## R-143 · Block-scaled AI number formats

*Gathered by a research subagent (Course 08 facts file, entries F-0807 and F-0808) and cross-checked by web search on 19 Nov 2026. The OCP and NVIDIA hosts could not be reached from the build environment, so every item below is from search-result excerpts of the named pages; re-check against the primary documents when they can be opened.*

- **OCP Microscaling Formats (MX) Specification v1.0** (September 2023), announced by OCP on 17 Oct 2023 on behalf of AMD, Arm, Intel, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Qualcomm: "The initial specification introduces four concrete floating point and integer-based data formats (MXFP8, MXFP6, MXFP4, and MXINT8)". Element types: MXFP8 E5M2 or E4M3, MXFP6 E3M2 or E2M3, MXFP4 E2M1, MXINT8. Every concrete format uses blocks of 32 elements sharing one 8-bit power-of-two scale (E8M0), so MXFP4 costs 4 + 8/32 = 4.25 bits per element. The block size and scale format were read from secondary documentation (pychop and Intel Neural Compressor docs), consistent across sources [Established]. **MX v1.1 (read 20 Nov 2026 from the PDF, primary):** "OCP MicroXcaling (MX) Specification Version 1.1", dated October 9, 2026. Its version history lists: "Description for conversion from vector of scalar elements to MX-compliant format in Section 6.3 updated"; "Renamed E8M0 to UE8M0"; "Refinements to FP8, FP6, and FP4 conversion modes and rounding terminology in Section 5.3"; "Clarifications of edge-cases for NaN (Section 5.1) and out-of-range (Sections 5.1, 6.1, 6.2) behavior". The concrete formats table is unchanged (MXFP8, MXFP6, MXFP4, MXINT8; block size 32; scale UE8M0, 8 bits). §6.3 adds an optional "expAdj(V) ∈ {0,1}" that "may be used to increase the scale factor by an additional power of two"; "If expAdj(V) is not implemented, a default 0 result is assumed." [OCP MX v1.1.0 (PDF)](https://www.opencompute.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OCP_MicroXcaling_Spec_v1.1.0.pdf). A second upload with a "-1" suffix exists; this entry uses the first.
- **NVIDIA NVFP4** (NVIDIA Technical Blog, "Introducing NVFP4 for Efficient and Accurate Low-precision Inference", June 2025): 4-bit E2M1 values (about −6 to 6), one FP8 E4M3 scale per 16-value block and a second-level FP32 scale per tensor: "This second-level scaling factor is done at a per-tensor level with FP32, which adjusts the original tensor's distribution such that the micro-blocks can be effectively encoded using E4M3 scale factors." About 4.5 bits per value [Established]. NVIDIA claims an accuracy loss of 1% or less against FP8 on its chosen benchmarks (DeepSeek-R1-0528) [Industry estimate: vendor claim].
- **Sources:** [OCP MX announcement](https://www.opencompute.org/blog/amd-arm-intel-meta-microsoft-nvidia-and-qualcomm-standardize-next-generation-narrow-precision-data-formats-for-ai); [OCP MX v1.0 specification](https://opencompute.org/documents/ocp-microscaling-formats-mx-v1-0-spec-final-pdf); [pychop MX documentation](https://pychop.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ocp_mx.html); [Intel Neural Compressor, Microscaling Quantization](https://intel.github.io/neural-compressor/latest/docs/source/3x/PT_MXQuant.html); [NVIDIA NVFP4 blog](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/introducing-nvfp4-for-efficient-and-accurate-low-precision-inference); [repost at edge-ai-vision.com](https://www.edge-ai-vision.com/2025/07/introducing-nvfp4-for-efficient-and-accurate-low-precision-inference/). Checked Nov 2026 (search excerpts).

## R-144 · DRAM error correction

*Course 08 facts file entries F-0813 and F-0814, cross-checked by web search on 19 Nov 2026; search-result excerpts only (JESD79-5 itself is paywalled).*

- **DDR5 on-die ECC:** Micron's *DDR5 New Features* white paper: "DDR5 SDRAM ECC is implemented as single error correction (SEC), pairing 128 data bits with 8 parity bits to form a 136-bit codeword." Academic papers describe it as a Hamming code with (n = 136, k = 128, d = 3), invisible to the system, able to miscorrect some double-bit errors into triple-bit errors, and separate from rank-level (side-band) ECC [Established].
- **JESD79-5C:** JEDEC announced the update on 17 Apr 2024: timings to 8800 Mbps, Per-Row Activation Counting (PRAC) against Rowhammer, and removal of Partial Array Self-Refresh for security reasons [Established]. Excerpts disagree on the previous speed ceiling, so none is quoted.
- **DDR5 module organization (added 19 Nov 2026 after the Course 08 audit):** the Wikipedia article *DDR5 SDRAM* (read directly): "Both subchannels on a DDR5 DIMM each have their own CA bus, controlling 32 bits for non-ECC memory and either 36 or 40 data lines for ECC memory, resulting in a total number of either 64, 72 or 80 data lines." DDR4 and earlier modules had one channel of 64 (non-ECC) or 72 (ECC) data lines [Established; secondary summary of JESD79-5, which is paywalled]. The Synopsys ECC bulletin (read directly) confirms that standard-DDR systems use side-band ECC on separate DRAMs and that on-die ECC is used "in conjunction with side-band ECC". The 25% overhead of 8 check bits per 32 data bits and the 7-bit SEC-DED requirement for 32 data bits are derived in 08-01.
- **Sources:** [Wikipedia, DDR5 SDRAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DDR5_SDRAM); [Micron DDR5 New Features white paper](https://www.micron.cn/content/dam/micron/global/public/products/white-paper/ddr5-new-features-white-paper.pdf); [Synopsys, Key Features of DDR5](https://www.synopsys.com/designware-ip/technical-bulletin/ddr5-features.html); [Synopsys, Error Correction Code (ECC) in DDR Memories](https://www.synopsys.com/designware-ip/technical-bulletin/error-correction-code-ddr.html); [Patel et al., DSN 2019](https://people.cs.rutgers.edu/~mp2099/files/patel_dsn19_understanding_paper.pdf); [JEDEC JESD79-5C release (Business Wire)](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240417886230/en/JEDEC-Updates-JESD79-5C-DDR5-SDRAM-Standard-Elevating-Performance-and-Security-for-Next-Gen-Technologies). Checked Nov 2026 (search excerpts).

## R-145 · Ethernet CRC-32

*Course 08 facts file entries F-0811 and F-0812, cross-checked by web search on 19 Nov 2026; search-result excerpts only.*

- **Frame check sequence:** IEEE 802.3 clause 3.2.9 uses G(x) = x³² + x²⁶ + x²³ + x²² + x¹⁶ + x¹² + x¹¹ + x¹⁰ + x⁸ + x⁷ + x⁵ + x⁴ + x² + x + 1 (04C11DB7₁₆ for the terms below x³²). The first 32 bits are complemented, M(x)·x³² is divided by G(x), and the remainder is complemented; the FCS covers addresses, length/type, data and pad. Quoted via Intel's Triple-Speed Ethernet IP user guide; the IEEE text itself was not read [Established].
- **Hamming distance:** P. Koopman, "32-Bit Cyclic Redundancy Codes for Internet Applications," IEEE DSN 2002, the first exhaustive search of 32-bit CRC polynomials: the IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 detects up to three independent bit errors in a 1500-byte payload (HD = 4), and other polynomials reach higher HD at those lengths [Established]. Taken from abstracts and excerpts; the paper's tables were not opened.
- **Sources:** [Intel Triple-Speed Ethernet IP user guide, CRC checking](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/programmable/683402/24-3/crc-checking.html); [Koopman 2002, CMU repository](https://kilthub.cmu.edu/articles/journal_contribution/32-Bit_Cyclic_Redundancy_Codes_for_Internet_Applications/6620594); [Koopman 2002, copy](https://typeset.io/pdf/32-bit-cyclic-redundancy-codes-for-internet-applications-1vyanily1r.pdf). Checked Nov 2026 (search excerpts).

## R-148 · Standard-cell library structure (SKY130)

*Read directly from the repositories with `git` on 19 Nov 2026 (the netlists were also read by the Course 08 research subagent, facts F-0815 to F-0818).*

- **SkyWater SKY130 high-density library (sky130_fd_sc_hd)**, repository google/skywater-pdk-libs-sky130_fd_sc_hd at commit ac7fb61f06e6470b94e8afdf7c25268f62fbd7b1 (10 Nov 2020) [Established]:
  - `inv_1`: "X0 VGND A Y VNB sky130_fd_pr__nfet_01v8 w=650000u l=150000u" and "X1 VPWR A Y VPB sky130_fd_pr__pfet_01v8_hvt w=1e+06u l=150000u": one nMOS and one high-threshold pMOS, 0.65 µm and 1.0 µm wide at 0.15 µm length (dimensions in µm under the PDK's scale convention).

  - `nand2_2` has 8 device lines (two copies of the NAND2); the library has nand2 in drives _1, _2, _4, _8 and inv in _1, _2, _4, _6, _8, _12, _16; the D flip-flop `dfxtp_1` has 24 device lines.

## R-155 · PRBS and LFSR references

*From search excerpts (vendor and IEEE pages unreachable from the build environment), Course 08 facts file entries F-0841 to F-0843; Swan's theorem from a search excerpt of a later paper's abstract. That each PRBS polynomial below is primitive, and that no degree-8 trinomial is irreducible, is proved independently by `verify_08_07.py`.*

- **Standard PRBS polynomials:** PRBS7 $x^7 + x^6 + 1$, PRBS15 $x^{15} + x^{14} + 1$, PRBS23 $x^{23} + x^{18} + 1$, PRBS31 $x^{31} + x^{28} + 1$, as tabulated in Intel's E-Tile Transceiver PHY User Guide ("Data Pattern Generation") and AMD transceiver documentation, which attribute them to ITU-T O.150 / O.151; several O.150 sequences are defined inverted [Established; search excerpts, tables not read verbatim].
- **IEEE 802.3 PRBS31:** defined as a test pattern for 10GBASE-R in clause 49.2.8; 802.3ae-era reflector discussion: "PRBS31 differs from O.150 in that for every 1 in O.150, D4.1 has a 0" (the same polynomial, bit-inverted). IEEE P802.3dj (2025) material carries PRBS31 and its PAM4 form PRBS31Q into the 200 Gb/s-per-lane generation [Established; search excerpts, the clause text itself not seen].
- **Xilinx XAPP052:** P. Alfke, "Efficient Shift Registers, LFSR Counters, and Long Pseudo-Random Sequence Generators", version 1.1, 7 July 1996, written for the XC4000; tabulates maximal-length taps up to 168 bits, "based on unpublished research done by Wayne Stahnke while he was at Fairchild Semiconductor in 1970" [Established; search excerpt of university copies, individual tap entries not checked against the PDF].
- **Swan's theorem:** R. G. Swan, "Factorization of polynomials over finite fields", *Pacific Journal of Mathematics* 12(3), 1962, pp. 1099–1106. A later abstract (Bluher) summarizes: Swan proved that trinomials $x^{8k} + x^m + 1$ with $8k > m$ have an even number of irreducible factors, so they cannot be irreducible [Established; summary from the later abstract, Swan's own statement not read].
- **Sources:** [Intel E-Tile PHY User Guide, Data Pattern Generation](https://intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/programmable/683723/current/data-pattern-generation.html); [AMD transceiver document](https://docs.amd.com/api/khub/documents/gYlAK_4raq3aAZ_rFGSPmQ/content); [IEEE 802.3dj presentation (Dudek, Mar 2025)](https://ieee802.org/3/dj/public/25_03/dudek_3dj_01_2503.pdf); [802.3ae reflector message](https://grouper.ieee.org/groups/802/3/10G_study/email/msg05450.html); [XAPP052, University of Idaho copy](https://www.webpages.uidaho.edu/~jfrenzel/440/Handouts/lfsr_XAPP052.pdf); [Swan 1962, Pacific J. Math.](https://msp.org/pjm/1962/12-3/p27.xhtml); [Bluher, arXiv math/0406538](https://www.arxiv.org/abs/math/0406538). Checked Nov 2026.

## R-156 · FSM synthesis and protocol state machines

*Yosys facts read from its repository with `git` (Course 08 facts file F-0845, F-0846); SKY130 `dfrtp_1` area read from the library's Liberty data with `git` on 19 Nov 2026; Vivado and PCIe facts from search excerpts (vendor and PCI-SIG pages unreachable from the build environment), F-0844 and two searches on 19 Nov 2026.*

- **Yosys FSM flow** (YosysHQ/yosys, commit d1338f8, `docs/source/using_yosys/synthesis/fsm.rst` and `passes/fsm/`): "The `fsm` command identifies, extracts, optimizes (re-encodes), and re-synthesizes finite state machines." `fsm_detect` marks a register as an FSM state register when it is not a module output, is driven by a single flip-flop cell, its next value comes from a multiplexer tree whose leaves are constants or the old state, and it is only compared with constants; `fsm_encoding = "none"` or `"auto"` suppresses or forces detection [Established].
- **Yosys automatic re-encoding** (`passes/fsm/fsm_recode.cc`): `encoding = GetSize(fsm_data.state_table) < 32 ? "one-hot" : "binary";` and "At the moment only one-hot encoding and binary encoding is supported." [Established].
- **AMD Vivado `FSM_ENCODING`** (UG901, UG912): values one_hot, sequential, johnson, gray, user_encoding, none and auto (the default, the tool chooses); "NONE disables state machine encoding within the Vivado synthesis tool for the specified state machine registers. In this case the state machine is synthesized as logic." [Established; search excerpts of the 2022–2023 guides].
- **AMD Vivado `FSM_SAFE_STATE`** (UG901 2025.2, UG912 2025.2): adds logic that detects an illegal state and moves the machine to a known state on the next cycle. `auto_safe_state` "Uses Hamming-3 encoding for auto-correction for one bit flip"; `reset_state`, `power_on_state` and `default_state` force the named state "using Hamming-2 encoding detection for one bit flip"; set on the state registers in RTL or XDC (`set_property fsm_safe_state reset_state [get_cells state_reg*]`). The value list differs between Vivado versions (2022.1 lists fewer values) [Established; search excerpts].
- **SkyWater SKY130 `sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfrtp_1`** (flip-flop with active-low asynchronous reset; google/skywater-pdk-libs-sky130_fd_sc_hd, commit ac7fb61, `cells/dfrtp/sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfrtp_1__tt_025C_1v80.lib.json`): area 25.024 µm² (the `nand2_1` is 3.7536 µm², R-154) [Established].
- **PCIe LTSSM:** a PCI Express textbook lists eleven top-level LTSSM states, Detect, Polling, Configuration, Recovery, L0, L0s, L1, L2, Hot Reset, Loopback and Disabled, with Detect the first state after a fundamental or hot reset; vendor documentation (Intel, TI, Efinix) lists sub-states such as Detect.Quiet and Polling.Active and exposes the current LTSSM state in monitor registers, with vendor-specific encodings [Established; search excerpts of secondary sources; the PCI-SIG base specification is members-only and was not read].
- **Sources:** [YosysHQ/yosys](https://github.com/YosysHQ/yosys); [AMD UG901 FSM_ENCODING (2023.1)](https://docs.amd.com/r/2023.1-English/ug901-vivado-synthesis/FSM_ENCODING); [AMD UG912 FSM_ENCODING](https://docs.amd.com/r/en-US/ug912-vivado-properties/FSM_ENCODING); [AMD UG901 FSM_SAFE_STATE (2025.2)](https://docs.amd.com/r/en-US/ug901-vivado-synthesis/FSM_SAFE_STATE); [AMD UG912 FSM_SAFE_STATE (2025.2)](https://docs.amd.com/r/2025.2-English/ug912-vivado-properties/FSM_SAFE_STATE); [sky130_fd_sc_hd repository](https://github.com/google/skywater-pdk-libs-sky130_fd_sc_hd); [PCI Express System Architecture, LTSSM section (O'Reilly)](https://oreilly.com/library/view/pci-express-system/0321156307/0321156307_ch14lev1sec6.html); [Intel PCIe IP user guide, LTSSM monitor registers](https://intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/programmable/683667/23-4/ltssm-monitor-registers.html); [Efinix LTSSM state encoding](https://www.efinixinc.com/docs-html/xcvr-pcie-controller-ug/topics/pcie/app-ltssm_state_encoding.html). ## R-157 · Arithmetic energy and DSP blocks

*Horowitz figure read directly from the paper (PDF downloaded with `curl` through the build environment's proxy on 19 Nov 2026 and its page rendered to an image, because the table is a figure); the other facts from search excerpts (Course 08 facts file F-0847 to F-0849, and a search on 19 Nov 2026).*

- **Energy per operation, 45 nm, 0.9 V** (M. Horowitz, "1.1 Computing's energy problem (and what we can do about it)", ISSCC 2014, DOI 10.1109/ISSCC.2014.6757323, Figure 1.1.9 "Rough energy costs for various operations in 45nm 0.9V"): integer add 8 bit 0.03 pJ, 32 bit 0.1 pJ; integer multiply 8 bit 0.2 pJ, 32 bit 3.1 pJ; floating-point add 16 bit 0.4 pJ, 32 bit 0.9 pJ; floating-point multiply 16 bit 1.1 pJ, 32 bit 3.7 pJ; 64-bit cache access 8 KB 10 pJ, 32 KB 20 pJ, 1 MB 100 pJ; DRAM 1.3–2.6 nJ; instruction energy breakdown about 70 pJ in total (I-cache access 25 pJ, register file 6 pJ, control, with the add a small sliver) [Established; read from the figure].
- **Kogge–Stone:** P. M. Kogge and H. S. Stone, "A Parallel Algorithm for the Efficient Solution of a General Class of Recurrence Equations," *IEEE Transactions on Computers* C-22(8), 786–793, Aug. 1973; recursive doubling "in time proportional to log2 N on a computer with N-fold parallelism" [Established; search excerpt].
- **Brent–Kung:** R. P. Brent and H. T. Kung, "A Regular Layout for Parallel Adders," *IEEE Transactions on Computers* C-31(3), 260–264, Mar. 1982 (earlier as CMU-CS-79-131, 1979): "addition of n-bit binary numbers can be done on a chip with a regular layout in time proportional to log n" [Established; search excerpt].
- **Prefix-network families:** D. Harris, "A taxonomy of parallel prefix networks" (IEEE Xplore document 1292373) describes a three-dimensional taxonomy of logic levels, fan-out and wiring tracks that places Kogge–Stone, Sklansky, Brent–Kung and the Knowles family in one space; S. Knowles, "A family of adders" (IEEE Symposium on Computer Arithmetic) [Established for the titles and authors; the years and venues were inconsistent across search excerpts (Knowles cited as 1999 and 2001), so the chapter gives no dates].
- **AMD DSP slices:** the UltraScale and UltraScale+ DSP48E2 has a 27 × 18 signed multiplier (25 × 18 in the 7-series DSP48E1), a 27-bit pre-adder and a 48-bit accumulator; UG974 calls it a "48-bit Multi-Functional Arithmetic Block"; the Versal DSP58 multiplier is 27 × 24 [Established; search excerpts of AMD documentation; UG579 itself not read].
- **Sources:** [Horowitz ISSCC 2014 (PDF copy)](https://www.gwern.net/doc/cs/hardware/2014-horowitz-2.pdf); [Kogge–Stone BibTeX record](https://researchr.org/publication/KoggeS73/bibtex); [Brent publication page](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~brent/pub/pub060.html); [Harris taxonomy, IEEE Xplore](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/1292373); [AMD DSP technology page](https://www.amd.com/en/products/adaptive-socs-and-fpgas/technologies/digital-signal-processing.html); [AMD UG974 DSP48E2](https://docs.amd.com/r/en-US/ug974-vivado-ultrascale-libraries/DSP48E2). Checked Nov 2026.

## R-158 · Metastability and synchronizers

*Beer and Ginosar papers read directly (PDFs downloaded with `curl` on 19 Nov 2026; τ values read from the 2012 paper's figures); Altera, Intel, AMD and Microchip facts from search excerpts (Course 08 facts file F-0851 to F-0855); Ginosar 2011 and Cummings 2002 bibliographic details from a search on 19 Nov 2026.*

- **MTBF law (Beer and Ginosar):** S. Beer and R. Ginosar, "A Model for Supply Voltage and Temperature Variation Effects on Synchronizer Performance," *IEEE Transactions on VLSI Systems* 23(11), 2461–2472, Nov. 2015, DOI 10.1109/TVLSI.2014.2365255. Equation (1): MTBF $= e^{S/\tau}/(T_W \times F_C \times F_D)$, with $F_C$ and $F_D$ the clock and data transition frequencies, $S$ the time allowed for resolution, $\tau$ the resolution time constant and $T_W$ "a vulnerable time window which is determined experimentally"; the abstract notes "degradation of MTBF with technology scaling for library flip-flop circuits in 65 nm and below" [Established; read from the paper].
- **Measured τ (Beer and Ginosar, 2012):** S. Beer and R. Ginosar, "A new 65nm LP metastability measurement test circuit," 2012 IEEE 27th Convention of Electrical and Electronics Engineers in Israel. Figures 5 and 6 plot the interpolated measured τ of a library flip-flop over 0.95–1.25 V and −20 to 100 °C: from below about 100 ps at the higher voltages and temperatures to roughly 700 ps at 0.95 V and −20 °C [Established; values read approximately from the paper's 3-D and color-map figures]. A search excerpt attributing to Beer and Ginosar the sentence "The τ measured on the 65nm circuit was about 100ps, in contrast with expectations of less than 30ps" was not found in either paper read, so the chapter does not use it.
- **Altera WP-01082,** "Understanding Metastability in FPGAs": MTBF $= e^{t_{MET}/C_2}/(C_1 f_{CLK} f_{DATA})$, where "The tMET parameter is the available metastability settling time, or the timing slack available beyond the registers tCO"; for a register chain, tMET is the sum of the per-register slacks; Quartus identifies synchronizer chains and reports MTBF [Established; search excerpts; the equation's typography reconstructed from the excerpt's description].
- **Intel Quartus Prime Pro design recommendations (25.1):** "designers commonly use two registers to synchronize a new signal, but a standard of three registers provides better metastability protection" (excerpt; may be paraphrased) [Established].
- **AMD XPM CDC macros (UG974, UG949):** DEST_SYNC_FF sets the number of destination synchronizer stages, from 2 to 10, default 4; "The value of this register influences MTBF, design size, and latency at the crossing point" [Established; search excerpts].
- **Microchip AN6287** (formerly AC474), "RTG4 and PolarFire Family Metastability Characterization Report," characterizes RTG4, PolarFire and RT PolarFire flip-flops with an MTBF model [Established; search excerpt; the measured values were not extracted].
- **Further-study references:** R. Ginosar, "Metastability and Synchronizers: A Tutorial," *IEEE Design & Test of Computers* 28(5), 23–35, 2011, DOI 10.1109/MDT.2011.113; C. E. Cummings, "Simulation and Synthesis Techniques for Asynchronous FIFO Design," SNUG San Jose 2002 [Established; search excerpts].
- **Sources:** [Beer and Ginosar 2015 (author copy)](https://webee.technion.ac.il/~ran/papers/VT-var-effects-on-Sync-BeerGinosar2015.pdf); [Beer and Ginosar 2012 (author copy)](https://webee.technion.ac.il/~ran/papers/BeerNew65nmLPMetastabilityMeasurmentIEEE-Israel2012.pdf); [Altera WP-01082](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/content-details/650346/understanding-metastability-in-fpgas.html); [Intel Quartus metastability analysis (25.1)](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/programmable/683082/25-1/metastability-analysis-in-the-software.html); [AMD UG974 XPM_CDC_SINGLE](https://docs.amd.com/r/2025.2-English/ug974-vivado-ultrascale-libraries/XPM_CDC_SINGLE); [AMD UG949 DEST_SYNC_FF](https://docs.amd.com/r/2023.1-English/ug949-vivado-design-methodology/Selecting-the-Correct-Value-for-the-DEST_SYNC_FF-Parameter); [Microchip AN6287](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/application-notes/an6287); [Ginosar 2011 (author copy)](https://www.ee.technion.ac.il/~ran/papers/Metastability-and-Synchronizers.IEEEDToct2011.pdf). Checked Nov 2026.

- **nextpnr** (YosysHQ/nextpnr, README at commit 0f387c6): "nextpnr aims to be a vendor neutral, timing driven, FOSS FPGA place and route tool"; supports iCE40 (Project IceStorm), ECP5 (Project Trellis), Nexus (Project Oxide), Gowin (Project Apicula), NanoXplore NG-Ultra and Cologne Chip GateMate; Cyclone V, MachXO2 and Xilinx 7-series (Project X-Ray) experimental; latest tag nextpnr-0.11.1 (commit dated 2026-08-10) [Established].
- **Project IceStorm** (YosysHQ/icestorm): "Project IceStorm aims at documenting the bitstream format of Lattice iCE40 FPGAs and providing simple tools for analyzing and creating bitstream files"; tag v1.1 created 2025-09-22 [Established].
- **Project Apicula** (YosysHQ/apicula): open Gowin bitstream tools, `pip install apycula`, used with Yosys and nextpnr-himbaechel; latest tag 0.35 (commit dated 2026-10-21) [Established].
- **Project X-Ray and F4PGA:** the prjxray README states that only Vivado 2017.2 works for its fuzzers ("**Is 2017.2 really required?** Yes, only `2017.2` works."); last commit 2025-06-05; the F4PGA top-level repository's last commit 2024-10-15 [Established]. That open flows are mature for small Lattice and Gowin parts and immature for large AMD and Altera parts is an interpretation of these facts [Industry estimate].
- **OpenROAD** (The-OpenROAD-Project/OpenROAD README at commit e1b501f): "The OpenROAD flow delivers an Autonomous, No-Human-In-Loop (NHIL) flow, 24 hour turnaround from RTL-GDSII"; quarterly release tags 26Q3 (2026-07-01) and 26Q4 (2026-10-01) [Established for the releases; the 24-hour figure is the project's own claim].
- **LibreLane** (librelane/librelane): "LibreLane is based on OpenLane 2 by Efabless Corporation (assets owned by UmbraLogic Technologies LLC)"; Apache-2.0, FOSSi Foundation trademark; stable tag 3.0.17 (2026-10-26) [Established].
- **Efabless and ChipFoundry:** Efabless, which ran the chipIgnite SKY130 multi-project-wafer shuttles used by Tiny Tapeout, shut down "Due to funding challenges" in the first quarter of 2025 (exact date unconfirmed); UmbraLogic Technologies LLC, operating as ChipFoundry, announced on 3 September 2025 that it had acquired Efabless's IP and technology assets [Established; search excerpts of several outlets].
- **iCE40 UltraPlus configuration time** (data sheet FPGA-DS-02008 v2.0, Table 4.23, "SPI Master or NVCM Configuration Time"): tCONFIG, POR/CRESET_B to device I/O active, maximum 140 ms at the default low frequency and 50 ms at medium frequency (the high-frequency value was blank in the extracted text); the family has internal non-volatile configuration memory (NVCM) and a 48 MHz high-frequency oscillator; the sysDSP block has "Optional independent pipeline control on Input Register, Output Register, and Intermediate Reg" [Established; read from the data sheet].
- **Sources:** [YosysHQ/yosys](https://github.com/YosysHQ/yosys); [YosysHQ/nextpnr](https://github.com/YosysHQ/nextpnr); [YosysHQ/icestorm](https://github.com/YosysHQ/icestorm); [YosysHQ/apicula](https://github.com/YosysHQ/apicula); [f4pga/prjxray](https://github.com/f4pga/prjxray); [chipsalliance/f4pga](https://github.com/chipsalliance/f4pga); [The-OpenROAD-Project/OpenROAD](https://github.com/The-OpenROAD-Project/OpenROAD); [librelane/librelane](https://github.com/librelane/librelane); [Tiny Tapeout news](https://tinytapeout.com/news/efabless-shutsdown/); [ChipFoundry release, GlobeNewswire](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/09/03/3143962/0/en/chipfoundry-acquires-efabless-assets-to-propel-custom-silicon-innovation.html); [iCE40 UltraPlus data sheet v2.0 (university copy)](https://pages.hmc.edu/brake/class/e155/fa23/assets/doc/FPGA-DS-02008-2-0-iCE40-UltraPlus-Family-Data-Sheet.pdf). ## R-161 · Crystal, band-structure and alloy parameters

*Read from downloaded copies of the handbook and the III–V compilation on 19 Nov 2026 (Course 09 facts file F-0901 to F-0914, F-0948); page images checked where the text extraction was garbled. Derived values are recomputed by `courses/09-semiconductor-devices/verify/verify_09_01.py`.*

- **Silicon (Levinshtein & Rumyantsev, §1.1–1.2):** "Effective electron masses … longitudinal 0.98 … transverse 0.19"; "Effective hole masses … heavy 0.49 … light 0.16"; "Electron affinity (eV) 4.05"; "Lattice constant (A) 5.431"; "Energy gap (eV) 1.12"; "Energy spin-orbital splitting (eV) 0.044"; "Effective conduction band density of states (cm⁻³) 3.2 x 10¹⁹", valence 1.8 × 10¹⁹; density-of-states masses "1.18 m0" (conduction, six valleys of 0.36 m0 each) and "mv = 0.81 m0 (300 K)"; conductivity mass 0.26 m0; split-off band mass 0.24 m0; Varshni fit "Eg = 1.17 − 4.73 × 10⁻⁴ T²/(T + 636) (eV)" (eq. 1.2.1) [Established].
- **Germanium (§2.1):** gap 0.661 eV; lattice constant 5.658 Å; density 5.3234 g/cm³; masses longitudinal 1.6, transverse 0.08, heavy hole 0.33, light hole 0.043 m0; four equivalent conduction valleys; electron affinity 4.0 eV [Established].
- **Gallium arsenide (§4.1–4.2):** gap 1.424 eV; electron mass 0.063 m0; heavy and light hole masses 0.51 and 0.082 m0; electron affinity 4.07 eV; Γ–L and Γ–X valley separations 0.29 and 0.48 eV; N_c 4.7 × 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ [Established].
- **Handbook mobilities (§1.1, §4.1):** lightly doped Si electrons ≤ 1400 and holes ≤ 450 cm²/V·s; GaAs electrons ≤ 8500 and holes ≤ 400 cm²/V·s [Established].
- **Vurgaftman, Meyer & Ram-Mohan (2001):** GaAs (Table I) a = 5.65325 Å, Γ gap 1.519 eV at 0 K, α = 0.5405 meV/K, β = 204 K, X gap 1.981 eV; electron mass "a low-temperature result of 0.067m0 at the band edge… At room temperature, the currently accepted value is 0.0635m0"; AlAs (Table II) a = 5.6611 Å, Γ gap 3.099 eV (α 0.885 meV/K, β 530 K), X gap 2.24 eV; InAs (Table III) a = 6.0583 Å, Γ gap 0.417 eV (α 0.276 meV/K, β 93 K); InP (Table VI) a = 5.8697 Å [Established].
- **AlGaAs (§V.A.1, Table XII):** "Bowing parameters from 0.14 to 0.66 eV have been proposed for the Γ-valley energy gap"; recommended C = (−0.127 + 1.310x) eV after Aspnes et al.; "Γ–X crossover composition of x = 0.38 at low temperatures (and 0.39 at 300 K)" [Established for a crossover near 0.4; Contested for the bowing]. Note: evaluating the recommended parameters directly puts the 0 K crossover nearer x ≈ 0.42, so the chapter quotes only "about 0.4" and makes no numerical AlGaAs gap claim. The often-quoted linear form E_g = 1.424 + 1.247x (x < 0.45), attributed to Casey and Panish, could not be read in a primary source (open issue).
- **GaInAs (§V.A.2):** "we choose a composite average of Eg(T=0) = 816 meV, which in turn implies a bowing parameter C = 0.477 eV" for Ga0.47In0.53As lattice-matched to InP; bowing assumed independent of temperature [Established]. Derived here: 0.7373 eV and 1682 nm at 300 K.
- **Wide-gap gaps:** GaN (wurtzite) 3.507 eV at 0 K with α = 0.909 meV/K, β = 830 K (Vurgaftman Table X), giving 3.435 eV at 300 K (derived); the Ioffe database lists 3.39 eV (search excerpt only); 4H-SiC 3.2, 3.23 or 3.26 eV (R-086) [Contested beyond the first decimal].
- **Hu, Table 1–4:** N_c 2.8 × 10¹⁹ and N_v 1.04 × 10¹⁹ cm⁻³ for Si; 1.04 × 10¹⁹ and 6.0 × 10¹⁸ for Ge; 4.7 × 10¹⁷ and 7.0 × 10¹⁸ for GaAs [Established].
- **Sources:** M. E. Levinshtein, S. L. Rumyantsev and M. S. Shur (eds.), *Handbook Series on Semiconductor Parameters, Vol. 1* (World Scientific, 1996), read from a library copy at [bdt.semi.ac.cn](https://bdt.semi.ac.cn/library/upload/files/2020/7/14133813301.pdf) (cite the book); [Vurgaftman et al., J. Appl. Phys. 89, 5815 (2001), course copy](https://ursemiconductors.web.illinois.edu/ECE536/Vurgaftman(2001).pdf), DOI 10.1063/1.1368156; [C. Hu, ch. 1–3](https://www.chu.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Chenming-Hu_ch1-3.pdf). Checked Nov 2026.

## R-162 · Wafer orientation, strain and wafer size

*Primary documents read on 19 Nov 2026 (Course 09 facts file F-0915 to F-0917, F-0920), plus Crossref bibliographic records for the Intel strained-silicon papers (titles, venues and pages only; the papers were not read).*

- **Orientation (Hu §1.1):** "silicon wafers are usually cut along the (100) plane to obtain uniformity and good device performance. A flat or a notch is cut along the (011) plane"; "Different surface orientations have different properties such as the rate of oxidation and the electronic quality of the oxide/semiconductor interface" [Established].
- **Mobility and orientation (Mooney, ECS Interface, Spring 2005):** "The highest electron mobility is found using Si(100) substrates; however, the highest hole mobility is observed when devices are fabricated in Si(110) substrates. These mobilities are for the <110> direction for both wafer orientations"; pFET drive current on bulk Si(110) "increased by 45% compared to control devices fabricated on Si(100)"; hybrid-orientation ring oscillators "with gate delay reduced by 21%" [Established; reported research results].
- **Strain (same article):** electron mobility enhancement "a factor of 1.5-2.0 for strain in the range of 0.4-1.0%"; "hole mobility enhancement factors are lower than for electrons, 1.0-1.4 for tensile strain in the range 1.0-1.9%"; uniaxial tensile strain "by the deposition of stressed silicon nitride films", and "SiGe grown selectively in the source and drain regions" compressing the pFET channel; bonded strained-Si-on-insulator threading dislocation density "about 5 x 10⁵ cm⁻²" in the best case. The article's opening motivates mobility enhancement by the growing difficulty of reducing "critical dimensions such as the gate oxide thickness" [Established].
- **Intel strained silicon (Crossref records):** S. E. Thompson et al., "A 90-nm logic technology featuring strained-silicon", IEEE TED 51(11), 1790–1797, Nov 2004, DOI 10.1109/TED.2004.836648; K. Mistry et al., "Delaying forever: Uniaxial strained silicon transistors in a 90nm CMOS technology", VLSI Symposium 2004, pp. 50–51, DOI 10.1109/VLSIT.2004.1345387; K. Mistry et al., "A 45nm Logic Technology with High-k+Metal Gate Transistors, Strained Silicon, …", IEDM 2007, pp. 247–250, DOI 10.1109/IEDM.2007.4418914 [Established for the titles; contents not read].
- **Wafer size:** IRDS 2024 Executive Summary: "the 300 mm wafer size conversion saw the demise of the 'One Billion Club.' During this wafer size conversion, the cost of a new factory rapidly escalated from the hundreds of million to over 1 billion" [Established]. Infineon (11 Sep 2024): "Chip production on 300 mm wafers is technologically more advanced and significantly more efficient compared to 200 mm wafers, since the bigger wafer diameter offers 2.3 times more chips per wafer" [Established]. The G450C 450 mm program faded in the mid-2010s without a production fab (search excerpts from Cadence and Semiconductor Engineering only; end date about 2016–2017 uncertain) [Industry estimate].
- **Sources:** [Hu ch. 1–3](https://www.chu.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Chenming-Hu_ch1-3.pdf); [Mooney 2005](https://www.electrochem.org/dl/interface/spr/spr05/IF03-05-Pg36-37.pdf); [Crossref record, Thompson 2004](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1109/ted.2004.836648); [Crossref record, Mistry 2004](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1109/vlsit.2004.1345387); [Crossref record, Mistry 2007](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1109/IEDM.2007.4418914); [IRDS 2024 Executive Summary](https://irds.ieee.org/images/files/pdf/2024/2024IRDS_ES.pdf); [Infineon, 300 mm GaN](https://www.infineon.com/regional/austria/press-release/2024/gan300); 450 mm excerpts: [Cadence Breakfast Bytes](https://community.cadence.com/cadence_blogs_8/b/breakfast-bytes/posts/450mm-wafers), [Semiconductor Engineering](https://semiengineering.com/450mm-silicon-wafer-issues-emerge). Checked Nov 2026.

## R-163 · Carrier statistics, dopants and dopant fluctuation

*Read from the downloaded handbook copy and Hu's chapters on 19 Nov 2026 (Course 09 facts file F-0907, F-0908, F-0948); the n_i history is in R-086. Derived values are recomputed by `courses/09-semiconductor-devices/verify/verify_09_02.py`.*

- **Silicon, 300 K (Levinshtein & Rumyantsev, §1.1–1.2):** "Intrinsic carrier concentration (cm⁻³) 1 x 10¹⁰"; "Intrinsic resistivity (Ω x cm) 3.2 x 10⁵"; "Effective conduction band density of states 3.2 x 10¹⁹", valence 1.8 × 10¹⁹ cm⁻³; "Dielectric constant 11.7"; mobilities "electrons < 1400 … holes < 450" cm²/V·s [Established].
- **Shallow dopants in silicon (§1.2.5):** "Ionization energies of shallow donors (eV) As 0.054, P 0.045, Sb 0.043"; "shallow acceptors (eV) Al 0.072, B 0.045, Ga 0.074, In 0.157" [Established].
- **Band-gap narrowing (§1.2.3):** "For 10¹⁷ < N_d < 3 x 10²⁰ cm⁻³, ΔE_g ≈ 3.5 x 10⁻⁸ · N_d^(1/3) (eV)", read from a figure caption on electrical and optical gap narrowing (Van Overstraeten and Mertens 1987) [Established as a fit; other narrowing models differ by tens of meV at the highest doping, Contested].
- **Germanium and GaAs (§2.1, §4.1):** Ge n_i 2.0 × 10¹³ cm⁻³; GaAs n_i 2.1 × 10⁶ cm⁻³ and static dielectric constant 12.9 [Established].
- **Hu, ch. 1:** Table 1–4 N_c, N_v for Ge, Si and GaAs (R-161); "n_i at room temperature is roughly 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ for Si and 10⁷ cm⁻³ for GaAs"; Table 1–3 conductivity masses (Si electrons 0.26, holes 0.39 m0) [Established].
- **Hu, ch. 7, §7.7 and §7.8:** "Yet another example of random variation is the random dopant fluctuation phenomenon. The statistical variation of the number of dopant atoms and their location in small size MOSFET creates significant variations in the threshold voltage"; for ultra-thin-body MOSFETs, small depletion widths "can be obtained without heavy channel doping, carrier mobility is improved"; for multigate MOSFETs, "There is no need for heavy doping in the channel to reduce Wdep. This leads to low vertical field and less impurity scattering; as a result the mobility is higher" [Established].
- **Derived here:** n_i = √(N_C N_V) e^(−E_g/2kT) = 9.39 × 10⁹ cm⁻³ from the handbook N_C, N_V and E_g = 1.12 eV (2.7% below Altermatt's 9.65 × 10⁹); hydrogenic donor 25.8 meV and 2.38 nm (m* = 0.26, ε_r = 11.7); course n_i(T) model rising 528-fold from 300 to 400 K; dopant counts in example transistor volumes.
- **Sources:** M. E. Levinshtein, S. L. Rumyantsev and M. S. Shur (eds.), *Handbook Series on Semiconductor Parameters, Vol. 1* (World Scientific, 1996), library copy at [bdt.semi.ac.cn](https://bdt.semi.ac.cn/library/upload/files/2020/7/14133813301.pdf) (cite the book); [C. Hu, ch. 1–3](https://www.chu.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Chenming-Hu_ch1-3.pdf); [C. Hu, ch. 7](https://www.chu.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Chenming-Hu_ch7.pdf). ## R-164 · Carrier transport in silicon

*Read from the downloaded handbook copy (page images of §1.3 checked to confirm exponents) and Hu's chapter 2 on 19 Nov 2026 (Course 09 facts file F-0909, F-0910). Derived values are recomputed by `courses/09-semiconductor-devices/verify/verify_09_03.py`.*

- **Mobility against doping at 300 K (Levinshtein & Rumyantsev, eqs. 1.3.1 and 1.3.4, after Baccarani and Ostoja 1975):** μ ≈ μ_min + (μ_max − μ_min)/[1 + (N/N_ref)^α]; electrons μ_min = 92, μ_max = 1360 cm²/V·s, α = 0.91, N_ref = 1.3 × 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ (10¹⁵ ≤ N_d ≤ 10²⁰ cm⁻³); holes μ_min = 48, μ_max = 450 cm²/V·s, α = 0.76, N_ref = 6.3 × 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ [Established as fits].
- **Lattice mobility (eqs. 1.3.2 and 1.3.5, after Dorkel and Leturcq 1981):** electrons μ ≈ 1430 (300/T)^2.2 cm²/V·s for N_d ≤ 10¹⁵ cm⁻³ and 250–600 K; holes μ_L = 495 (300/T)^2.2 [Established].
- **Velocity against field (eqs. 1.3.6, 1.3.8, 1.3.9, after Jacoboni et al. 1977):** v_d ≈ v_s (F/F_c)/[1 + (F/F_c)^β]^(1/β); electrons (F ∥ ⟨111⟩, N_d ≤ 10¹⁶ cm⁻³, T > 250 K) v_s = 1.53 × 10⁹ T^−0.87 cm/s, F_c = 1.01 T^1.55 V/cm, β = 2.57 × 10⁻² T^0.66; holes (F ∥ ⟨100⟩) v_s ≈ 1.62 × 10⁸ T^−0.52 cm/s, F_c = 1.24 T^1.68 V/cm, β = 0.46 T^0.17 [Established].
- **Other silicon values (§1.1):** electron and hole thermal velocities 2.3 × 10⁵ and 1.65 × 10⁵ m/s; optical phonon energy 0.063 eV; diffusion coefficients ≤ 36 (electrons) and ≤ 12 cm²/s (holes); hole Hall factor about 0.75–0.9 at 300 K across 10¹⁴–10¹⁸ cm⁻³ (Fig. 1.3.9, Lin et al. 1981) [Established].
- **Hu, ch. 2:** Table 2–1, lightly doped mobilities at room temperature: Si 1400/470, Ge 3900/1900, GaAs 8500/400, InAs 30 000/500 cm²/V·s (electrons/holes); fits μ_p = 420/[1 + ((N_a + N_d)/1.6 × 10¹⁷)^0.7] + 50 and μ_n = 1318/[1 + ((N_a + N_d)/10¹⁷)^0.85] + 92 (Eqs. 2.2.8–2.2.9, read from the page image); "In small devices, the electric field can easily reach 10⁵ V/cm … electron and hole velocities saturate at around 10⁷ cm/s"; "Mobility and even velocity saturation … are concepts that … become fuzzy when we deal with devices whose sizes are smaller than the mean free path"; "it is not easy to measure mobility accurately and that we should presume the existence of uncertainties in experimental data in general" [Established].
- **Derived here:** the two fits agree within 6.8% for electrons over 10¹⁵–10¹⁹ cm⁻³ but differ by up to 55% for holes near 7 × 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ [Contested]; low-field mobility of the Jacoboni electron fit 1534 cm²/V·s at 300 K; D_n = 34.77 cm²/s at 10¹⁵ cm⁻³ by the Einstein relation.
- **Sources:** M. E. Levinshtein, S. L. Rumyantsev and M. S. Shur (eds.), *Handbook Series on Semiconductor Parameters, Vol. 1* (World Scientific, 1996), library copy at [bdt.semi.ac.cn](https://bdt.semi.ac.cn/library/upload/files/2020/7/14133813301.pdf) (cite the book); [C. Hu, ch. 2](https://www.chu.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Chenming-Hu_ch2-2.pdf). Checked Nov 2026.

## R-165 · Recombination parameters and solar-cell records

*Handbook values read from page images of the downloaded copy on 19 Nov 2026 (§1.2 deep-level table, §1.3.4); solar-cell records from the Course 09 facts file (F-0945, F-0946), read from the primary documents by the fact-finder. Derived values are recomputed by `courses/09-semiconductor-devices/verify/verify_09_04.py`.*

- **Silicon recombination coefficients (Levinshtein & Rumyantsev, §1.3.4):** radiative "1.1 x 10⁻¹⁴ cm³ s⁻¹" at 300 K (Gerlach et al. 1972); Auger "C_n 1.1 x 10⁻³⁰, C_p 0.3 x 10⁻³⁰, C = C_n + C_p 1.4 x 10⁻³⁰ cm⁶ s⁻¹" at 300 K, with C ≈ 1.4 × 10⁻³⁰ (T/300)^0.5 for 180–400 K [Established].
- **Surface recombination (§1.3.4):** "Surface recombination rate depending on treatment of Si surface lies in the range between 10² ÷ (6–8) x 10⁴ cm s⁻¹. Surface recombination rate on the Si-SiO₂ interface can be as small as ≤ 0.5 cm s⁻¹" [Established].
- **Lifetime against doping (Figs. 1.3.22–1.3.23):** hole lifetime in n-type and electron lifetime in p-type silicon fall from about 10⁻³ s at 10¹²–10¹³ cm⁻³ ("numerous experimental data for good quality industrial produced" silicon) to about 10⁻⁹ s near 10²⁰ cm⁻³ (Alamo and Swanson 1987; Tyagi and Van Overstraeten 1983), read approximately from the log plots [Established at the order-of-magnitude level].
- **Deep levels with impurities (§1.2, table):** Au donor E_v + 0.35 eV (σ_n 10⁻¹⁵, σ_p 3.5 × 10⁻¹⁵ cm²) and acceptor E_c − 0.55 eV (σ_n 8 × 10⁻¹⁷, σ_p 9.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ cm²); Cu, Fe (E_v + 0.39 eV), Ni, Pt (acceptor E_c − 0.25 eV, σ_n 5 × 10⁻¹⁴) and Zn levels; radiation-defect levels (A-center E_c − 0.17 eV, E-center E_c − 0.45 eV, divacancy levels) [Established].
- **GaAs (§4.1):** radiative recombination coefficient "7 x 10⁻¹⁰" cm³/s [Established].
- **Hu, ch. 2, §2.6–2.8:** recombination lifetime; "In silicon, direct recombination is unimportant and the lifetime is highly variable and determined by the density of recombination centers"; quasi-Fermi levels, with electrons and holes "only loosely coupled by the recombination/generation mechanism, which is a slow process (has a long time constant around 1 µs)" while intra-band scattering has "0.1 ps mean free time" [Established].
- **Solar-cell records:** Fraunhofer ISE, *Photovoltaics Report* (updated 14 July 2026), citing Solar Cell Efficiency Tables version 68 (May 2026): "The record lab cell efficiency is 28.1% for monocrystalline wafer-based technology" [Established]. LONGi (September 2026): a hybrid interdigitated back-contact cell "has attained a photoelectric conversion efficiency of 28.29%, verified by Institute for Solar Energy Research Hamelin (ISFH)", described as 96.2% of the theoretical limit, implying about 29.4% [Contested: company claim, not yet independently tabulated].
- **Sources:** M. E. Levinshtein, S. L. Rumyantsev and M. S. Shur (eds.), *Handbook Series on Semiconductor Parameters, Vol. 1* (World Scientific, 1996), library copy at [bdt.semi.ac.cn](https://bdt.semi.ac.cn/library/upload/files/2020/7/14133813301.pdf) (cite the book); [C. Hu, ch. 2](https://www.chu.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Chenming-Hu_ch2-2.pdf); [Fraunhofer ISE Photovoltaics Report](https://www.ise.fraunhofer.de/content/dam/ise/de/documents/publications/studies/Photovoltaics-Report.pdf); [LONGi release](https://www.longi.com/en/news/isfh-hibc-crystalline-silicon-cell-efficiency/). Checked Nov 2026.

## R-166 · Junction electrostatics references

*Read from the downloaded handbook copy and Hu's chapters 4 and 7 on 19 Nov 2026. Derived values are recomputed by `courses/09-semiconductor-devices/verify/verify_09_05.py`.*

- **Silicon (Levinshtein & Rumyantsev, §1.1):** "Dielectric constant 11.7"; "Breakdown field (V cm⁻¹) ~ 3 x 10⁵" [Established as an order of magnitude; the handbook also gives breakdown voltage and field against doping for abrupt junctions, so the value varies with doping].
- **Other materials (§2.1, §4.1, §3.1):** breakdown field about 10⁵ V/cm for Ge, about 4 × 10⁵ V/cm for GaAs, and 10⁶–10⁷ V/cm reported for diamond; GaAs static dielectric constant 12.9 [Established].
- **Hu, ch. 4, §4.4:** "PN junction is prevalent in semiconductor devices and its capacitance is an unwelcome capacitive load to the devices and the circuits. C_dep can be lowered by reducing the junction area and increasing W_dep by reducing the doping concentration(s) and/or applying a reverse bias. Numerically, C ≈ 1 fF/µm² when W_dep = 0.1 µm"; the 1/C² against voltage plot gives doping and built-in potential [Established].
- **Hu, ch. 7, §7.8 (SOI):** "SOI provides a speed advantage because the source/drain to body junction capacitance is practically eliminated as the source and drain diffusion regions extend vertically to the buried oxide. The cost of an SOI wafer is higher than an ordinary Si wafer" [Established].
- **Derived here:** the one-sided-junction relations V_br ≈ ε_s E_c²/(2qN), W = 2V_br/E_c and the drift-region resistance per area 4V_br²/(ε_s μ E_c³) (the "silicon limit"), evaluated for 200 V and 600 V with E_c = 3 × 10⁵ V/cm and the 09-03 mobility model; the full Poisson solution of a 10¹⁷/10¹⁶ cm⁻³ junction (half-density width 0.3118 µm against 0.3318 µm in the depletion approximation).

Shur (eds.), *Handbook Series on Semiconductor Parameters, Vol. 1* (World Scientific, 1996), library copy at [bdt.semi.ac.cn](https://bdt.semi.ac.cn/library/upload/files/2020/7/14133813301.pdf) (cite the book); [C. ## R-180 · Image-sensor pixel readout

*Read on 19 Nov 2026; corrected 20 Nov 2026 after the Course 10 audit. The primary papers could not be downloaded. The Wikipedia article cites Fossum and Hondongwa only for the pinned photodiode; its four-transistor pixel description is cited to C.-i. Lin, C.-H. Lai and Y.-C. King, "A four transistor CMOS active pixel sensor with high dynamic range operation," Proc. 2004 IEEE Asia-Pacific Conf. on Advanced System Integrated Circuits, pp. 124–127, doi:10.1109/APASIC.2004.1349425 (not read). The same article states that "shared-row, four-ways and eight-ways shared read out, and other architectures can be employed" to increase pixel density, so not every pixel has its own source follower. Tagged [Established] because the 4T pixel structure is standard textbook and review material.*

- **4T active pixel:** a pinned photodiode, a floating diffusion and four transistors (transfer gate, reset gate, selection gate and a source-follower readout transistor); the source follower buffers the pixel voltage onto the column without removing the accumulated charge [Established]. Primary source: E. R. Fossum and D. B. Hondongwa, "A Review of the Pinned Photodiode for CCD and CMOS Image Sensors," *IEEE J. Electron Devices Society*, vol. 2, no. 3, pp. 33–43, 2014, doi:10.1109/JEDS.2014.2306412. Read via [Wikipedia, "Active-pixel sensor"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active-pixel_sensor). Used in 10-06. See open issue 39.

## R-181 · Transistor matching

*Bibliographic record confirmed on 19 Nov 2026 through the Crossref API (title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, date, DOI); the paper itself was not opened (IEEE Xplore refuses automated access). The area law is the paper's widely cited result and standard textbook material. Tagged [Established].*

- **Pelgrom, Duinmaijer and Welbers, "Matching properties of MOS transistors,"** *IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits*, vol. 24, no. 5, pp. 1433–1439, Oct. 1989, doi:10.1109/JSSC.1989.572629: the standard deviation of the parameter difference between closely spaced, identically drawn transistors scales as 1/√(WL), σ(ΔV_TH) = A_VT/√(WL) [Established]. A 1988 ESSCIRC paper of the same title by Pelgrom and Duinmaijer also exists (doi:10.1109/ESSCIRC.1988.5468276). The A_VT value used in 10-08 (3.5 mV·µm) is illustrative, not a specific process's figure. Used in 10-08.

## R-187 · IIR filter implementations

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 from Arm's online documentation (the "latest" pages at the URLs below). Library statements are tagged [Established] as the library's documented behavior.*

- **Arm CMSIS-DSP, "Biquad Cascade IIR Filters Using Direct Form I Structure"**: "This set of functions implements arbitrary order recursive (IIR) filters. The filters are implemented as a cascade of second order Biquad sections. The functions support Q15, Q31 and floating-point data types." Each stage implements "y[n] = b0 * x[n] + b1 * x[n-1] + b2 * x[n-2] + a1 * y[n-1] + a2 * y[n-2]"; "A Direct Form I algorithm is used with 5 coefficients and 4 state variables per stage." "Pay careful attention to the sign of the feedback coefficients. Some design tools use the difference equation … - a1 * y[n-1] - a2 * y[n-2]. In this case the feedback coefficients a1 and a2 must be negated when used with the CMSIS DSP Library." An 8th-order filter uses numStages = 4; a 9th-order filter uses 5 stages with one configured as first order (b2 = 0, a2 = 0) [Established]. Used in 11-04. [Documentation](https://arm-software.github.io/CMSIS-DSP/latest/group__BiquadCascadeDF1.html).
- **Arm CMSIS-DSP, "Biquad Cascade IIR Filters Using a Direct Form II Transposed Structure"**: implements the same cascades "using a transposed direct form II structure"; "These functions provide a slight memory savings as compared to the direct form I Biquad filter functions"; two state values d1, d2 per stage; the same sign warning; and, on the numerical choice: "The advantage of the Direct Form I structure is that it is numerically more robust for fixed-point data types. That is why the Direct Form I structure supports Q15 and Q31 data types. The transposed Direct Form II structure, on the other hand, requires a wide dynamic range for the state variables d1 and d2. Because of this, the CMSIS library only has a floating-point version of the Direct Form II Biquad. The advantage of the Direct Form II Biquad is that it requires half the number of state variables, 2 rather than 4, per Biquad stage" [Established]. Used in 11-04. [Documentation](https://arm-software.github.io/CMSIS-DSP/latest/group__BiquadCascadeDF2T.html).
- **Arm CMSIS-DSP, "Finite Impulse Response (FIR) Filters"** (group page, read 20 Nov 2026): lists processing functions `arm_fir_f16`, `arm_fir_f32` and `arm_fir_f64` ("Processing function for floating-point FIR filter") and `arm_fir_q7`, `arm_fir_q15` and `arm_fir_q31` for fixed point [Established]. Used in 11-07. [FIR documentation](https://arm-software.github.io/CMSIS-DSP/latest/group__FIR.html).

## R-189 · SerDes reference equalizer

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 from the IEEE P802.3ck task force's public tools page: the COM 3.70 archive (`mellitz_3ck_adhoc_01_032322_COM3p70.zip`) was downloaded and its MATLAB source and configuration workbook opened. These are task-force tools and draft configurations, not the published standard; the values in IEEE Std 802.3ck-2022 itself were not checked (the standard was not accessible here).*

- **COM source, `com_ieee8023_93a_370.m`** [Established, as code]: function `FD_CTLE` computes `hctf = ( 10.^(kacdc_dB/20) + 1i*freq/f_z ) ./ ( (1+1i*freq/f_p1) .* (1+1i*freq/f_p2))`, i.e. $H(f) = (G + jf/f_z)/[(1 + jf/f_{p1})(1 + jf/f_{p2})]$ with $G = 10^{g_{DC}/20}$; the time-domain version maps the poles to $-2\pi f_{p1}$, $-2\pi f_{p2}$ and the zero to $-2\pi f_zG$. A second stage, `H_low = (10.^(g_DC_HP/20) + 1i*f/f_HP)./(1 + 1i*f/f_HP)`, adds a low-frequency pole–zero pair.
- **Configuration `config_com_ieee8023_93a=3ck_d3p1_KR_11_30_21.xlsx`** (draft 3.1, 30 Nov 2021; distributed with COM 3.70, March 2022) [Established, as a draft configuration]: `f_b` 53.125 GBd; `g_DC` [−20:1:0] dB; `f_z` 21.25 GHz; `f_p1` 21.25 GHz; `f_p2` 53.125 GHz; `g_DC_HP` [−6:1:0]; `f_HP_PZ` 0.6640625 GHz (= f_b/80).. The CR_CA and 120F_C2C configurations of the same draft set the same CTLE values; the C2M and MTF (host-to-module) configurations set `g_DC` [−13:1:0], `f_z` 12.58 GHz, `f_p1` 20 GHz, `f_p2` 28 GHz, `g_DC_HP` [−3:0.5:0] and `f_HP_PZ` 1.328125 GHz (re-read from the workbooks' cell XML, 20 Nov 2026). Used in 11-08 and 11-09.
- **Digital implementation** [Established, as code]: function `TD_CTLE` (comment: "Equation 93A-22 implemented in z-space") maps each pole and the zero with `(1+p/bilinear_fs)./(1-p/bilinear_fs)`, where `bilinear_fs = 2*fb*oversampling` (the bilinear transform with 2/T, T = 1/(f_b·M)), and builds the numerator as `poly([zd, -1])`, i.e. with an extra zero at z = −1; the call passes `param.samples_per_ui`, read as `xls_parameter(parameter, 'M', 32)`, and the KR configuration sets `M` = 32. Used in 11-09.
- **Source:** [IEEE P802.3ck tools page](https://www.ieee802.org/3/ck/public/tools/index.html), COM version 3.70 (R. Mellitz, posted March 2022). Checked Nov 2026.

The internal RS resistor is accurate to 15% so actual bandwidth will vary"; "A larger value CFILTER capacitor can be used for increased attenuation at higher frequencies for anti-aliasing purposes … The tradeoff is that a larger capacitor value gives degraded THD performance." §8.3.4.3: a "second-order modulator"; "the sampling clock has a typical value of 128 kHz"; the on-chip decimation filters "also provide antialias filtering". §8.3.5: "The sinc filter has notches (or zeroes) that occur at the output data rate and multiples thereof"; "the … passband repeats itself at every fMOD. ## R-196 · RF exposure limits (FCC and ICNIRP)

*Re-read on 20 Nov 2026 to extend R-083 with the full US maximum-permissible-exposure table; values tagged [Established] as regulation and published guidelines.*

- **47 CFR § 1.1310(e)(1), Table 1** (eCFR text read 20 Nov 2026), "(ii) Limits for General Population/Uncontrolled Exposure": "30-300 27.5 0.073 0.2 <30" (frequency MHz; electric field V/m; magnetic field A/m; power density mW/cm²; averaging time minutes), "300-1,500 f/1500 <30", "1,500-100,000 1.0 <30". § 1.1310(c): "a peak spatial-average SAR of 1.6 W/kg, averaged over any 1 gram of tissue (defined as a tissue volume in the shape of a cube)". [eCFR § 1.1310](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-1/subpart-I/section-1.1310)
- **ICNIRP 2020**, *Health Physics* 118(5):483–524, Table 2 (basic restrictions, averaging intervals ≥ 6 min), general public: 100 kHz to 6 GHz whole-body 0.08 W/kg, local head/torso 2 W/kg, local limb 4 W/kg; above 6 GHz to 300 GHz, absorbed power density 20 W/m²; "Local SAR is to be averaged over a 10-g cubic mass". [ICNIRP 2020 (PDF)](https://www.icnirp.org/cms/upload/publications/ICNIRPrfgdl2020.pdf)
- **Derived here (13-04):** the ratio 27.5 V/m ÷ 0.073 A/m = 376.7 Ω (the plane-wave impedance the table assumes); the rms field of a 10 W/m² plane wave, √(10 × 376.7) = 61.38 V/m; the far-field distance at which 1 W EIRP gives 10 W/m², 8.92 cm.

## R-201 · RISC-V unprivileged ISA manual, version 20260120

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 from RISC-V International's ratified specifications library (primary); tagged [Established].*

- **Versions:** the manual set is versioned by date; 20260120 is current (earlier: 20250508, 20240411). The unprivileged preface lists "RV32I 2.1 Ratified … RV64I 2.1 Ratified"; the privileged volume lists Machine ISA 1.13 and Supervisor ISA 1.13. [Unprivileged preface](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/unpriv/colophon.html) · [Privileged preface](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/priv/priv-preface.html)
- **RV32I chapter:** "RV32I contains 40 unique instructions"; "The RISC-V ISA keeps the source (rs1 and rs2) and destination (rd) registers at the same position in all formats to simplify decoding"; "the sign bit for all immediates is always in bit 31 of the instruction to speed sign-extension circuitry"; "The conditional branch range is ±4 KiB"; "Jumps can therefore target a ±1 MiB range"; "NOP is encoded as ADDI x0, x0, 0"; ADDI with rd = x0 (other than the NOP) is listed among the HINT encodings. [RV32I chapter](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/unpriv/rv32.html)
- **Endianness (Introduction):** "RISC-V base ISAs have either little-endian or big-endian memory systems, with the privileged architecture further defining bi-endian operation. Instructions are stored in memory as a sequence of 16-bit little-endian parcels, regardless of memory system endianness." [Introduction](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/unpriv/intro.html)
- **C extension:** "Typically, 50%-60% of the RISC-V instructions in a program can be replaced with RVC instructions, resulting in a 25%-30% code-size reduction." [C extension](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/unpriv/c-st-ext.html)
- **Derived here (14-02):** every encoding, range and code size in the chapter is reproduced with LLVM 18's `llvm-mc` in verify_14_02.py.
- **Control-flow integrity (Chapter 34, "Control-flow Integrity (CFI)"; read 20 Nov 2026 for the Course 14 audit):** "To enforce forward-edge control-flow integrity, the Zicfilp extension introduces a landing pad (LPAD) instruction." "Compilers emit a landing pad instruction as the first instruction of an address-taken function, as well as at any indirect jump targets." "The Zicfiss extension introduces a shadow stack to enforce backward-edge control-flow integrity." "A shadow stack is a second stack used to store a shadow copy of the return address in the link register if it needs to be spilled." [Control-flow Integrity](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/unpriv/unpriv-cfi.html)

## R-208 · Energy per operation at 45 nm (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014)

*A re-check of [R-157](#r-157--arithmetic-energy-and-dsp-blocks), which first logged this table (read from the paper itself); the values agree.*

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 from a third-party mirror of the published digest pages (secondary copy; the IEEE footer and page numbers match the digest), not from IEEE Xplore; tagged [Established] as the field's standard reference table, with the caveat below.*

- **Figure 1.1.9, "Rough energy costs for various operations in 45nm 0.9V":** integer add 8-bit 0.03 pJ, 32-bit 0.1 pJ; integer multiply 8-bit 0.2 pJ, 32-bit 3.1 pJ; FP add 16-bit 0.4 pJ, 32-bit 0.9 pJ; FP multiply 16-bit 1.1 pJ, 32-bit 3.7 pJ; 64-bit cache read 8 KB 10 pJ, 32 KB 20 pJ, 1 MB 100 pJ; DRAM 1.3–2.6 nJ.
- **Text:** "the programmable nature of a processor has high energy overhead, 70pJ/instruction, vs. a few pJ for an operation"; "energy cost of a DRAM access (1 to 2nJ) is a couple of orders-of-magnitude higher than the cost of an internal cache access or functional operation (10pJ)".
- **Caveat:** the paper's table (1.3–2.6 nJ) and text (1 to 2 nJ) disagree on DRAM; quote the one used and attribute it.
- M. Horowitz, "1.1 Computing's energy problem (and what we can do about it)", ISSCC 2014 Digest of Technical Papers, pp. 10–14, doi:10.1109/ISSCC.2014.6757323. Copy read: [mirror (PDF)](https://gwern.net/doc/cs/hardware/2014-horowitz-2.pdf)

## R-209 · RISC-V ELF psABI: calling convention, relocations and relaxation

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 from the psABI source files on the master branch of RISC-V International's riscv-elf-psabi-doc repository (primary); tagged [Established].*

- **Calling conventions (riscv-cc.adoc):** the integer register table (x0 zero; x1 ra, not preserved; x2 sp, preserved; x3 gp and x4 tp, unallocatable; x5–x7 t0–t2, not preserved; x8–x9 s0–s1, preserved; x10–x17 a0–a7, not preserved; x18–x27 s2–s11, preserved; x28–x31 t3–t6, not preserved); "The base integer calling convention provides eight argument registers, a0-a7, the first two of which are also used to return values."; "The stack grows downwards (towards lower addresses) and the stack pointer shall be aligned to a 128-bit boundary upon procedure entry."; "Registers s0-s11 shall be preserved across procedure calls."; the ILP32 type table (char 1, short 2, int 4, long 4, long long 8, void * 4, double 8, each aligned to its size); LP64 makes long and pointers 8 bytes. [riscv-cc.adoc](https://github.com/riscv-non-isa/riscv-elf-psabi-doc/blob/master/riscv-cc.adoc)
- **ELF object files (riscv-elf.adoc):** "R_RISCV_CALL and R_RISCV_CALL_PLT relocations are associated with pairs of instructions (AUIPC+JALR) generated by the CALL or TAIL pseudoinstructions"; "With linker relaxation enabled, the AUIPC instruction in the AUIPC+JALR pair has both a R_RISCV_CALL or R_RISCV_CALL_PLT relocation and an R_RISCV_RELAX relocation"; "Procedure call linker relaxation allows the AUIPC+JALR pair to be relaxed to the JAL instruction when the procedure or PLT entry is within (-1MiB to +1MiB-2) of the instruction pair." [riscv-elf.adoc](https://github.com/riscv-non-isa/riscv-elf-psabi-doc/blob/master/riscv-elf.adoc)
- **Derived here (14-03):** every listing, relocation, address and layout in the chapter is reproduced with LLVM 18 (llvm-mc, ld.lld, clang) in verify_14_03.py.

## R-210 · Number formats: IEEE 754-2019, bfloat16 and OCP MX (primary re-check)

*Read on 20 Nov 2026; primary sources, tagged [Established]. Re-checks and extends [R-056](#r-056--low-precision-floating-point-formats) and [R-143](#r-143--block-scaled-ai-number-formats), whose MX details had come from secondary documentation.*

- **IEEE 754-2019:** IEEE SA standard page: "Active Standard IEEE 754-2019 … Superseding 754-2008 … Board Approval 2019-06-13 … Published: 2019-07-22"; an active revision project, P754, is listed. Identical adoption: ISO/IEC/IEEE 60559:2020. [IEEE SA](https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/)
- **bfloat16:** Google Cloud Blog (S. Wang and P. Kanwar, 23 Aug 2019): "Bfloat16 is a custom 16-bit floating point format for machine learning that's comprised of one sign bit, eight exponent bits, and seven mantissa bits"; "bfloat16 multipliers are about half the size in silicon of a typical FP16 multiplier, and they are eight times smaller than an FP32 multiplier!" Google Cloud TPU documentation (updated Nov 2026): "By default, TPUs perform matrix multiplication operations with bfloat16 values and accumulations with IEEE float32 values"; "the bfloat16 on Cloud TPU does not support subnormals, so all subnormals are flushed to zero during the conversion." RISC-V's ratified BF16 extensions note that BF16 "is not an IEEE-754 standard format" but a valid format under IEEE 754's rules. [Google blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/bfloat16-the-secret-to-high-performance-on-cloud-tpus) · [Cloud TPU docs](https://cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/bfloat16) · [RISC-V BF16 chapter](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/unpriv/bfloat16.html)
- **OCP MX v1.0 (Sep 2023), read directly:** contributors AMD, Arm, Intel, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Qualcomm; MXFP8 (E5M2/E4M3), MXFP6 (E3M2/E2M3), MXFP4 (E2M1) and MXINT8, each with k = 32 and an E8M0 scale; "each block of k elements can be encoded in (w + kd) bits"; E8M0 has no Inf and a single NaN; E2M1 has bias 1, maximum ±6.0, no Inf or NaN. §6.1–6.2: the dot product's "internal precision … and order of operations is implementation-defined". §6.3 conversion: "Set X to be the largest power-of-two less than or equal to max(|Vi|), divided by the largest power-of-two representable in the element data type"; elements are quantized with roundTiesToEven, and normal numbers beyond the element maximum are clamped. MXINT8 elements carry an implicit scale (one sign bit, one integer bit, six fractional bits). [OCP MX v1.0 (PDF)](https://www.opencompute.org/documents/ocp-microscaling-formats-mx-v1-0-spec-final-pdf)
- **RISC-V M and F chapters (manual 20260120):** division by zero returns an all-ones quotient and the dividend as remainder; signed overflow returns the dividend and remainder 0; rounding modes RNE, RTZ, RDN, RUP, RMM; canonical NaN 0x7fc00000; tininess detected after rounding (see R-201 for the manual).
- **Derived here (14-04):** the p² multiplier-area model (bfloat16 about half of FP16 and a ninth of FP32), consistent with Google's statements; all arithmetic results are machine-checked in verify_14_04.py.

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 (primary: the Project Zero post and the MITRE CVE records; NVD returned 403); tagged [Established].*

- J. Horn, Google Project Zero, "Reading privileged memory with a side-channel", 3 Jan 2018: "We reported this issue to Intel, AMD and ARM on 2017-06-01"; "Variant 1: bounds check bypass (CVE-2017-5753) Variant 2: branch target injection (CVE-2017-5715) Variant 3: rogue data cache load (CVE-2017-5754)". - CVE-2017-5753 description: "Systems with microprocessors utilizing speculative execution and branch prediction may allow unauthorized disclosure of information to an attacker with local user access via a side-channel analysis." Records reserved 2017-02-01, public 2018-01-03, published 2018-01-04 (CNA: Intel). [CVE-2017-5753](https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2017-5753) · [CVE-2017-5715](https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2017-5715) · [CVE-2017-5754](https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2017-5754)

- **Later variant, read 20 Nov 2026 for the Course 14 audit (primary, MITRE CVE records):** CVE-2022-29900 (published 2022-07-12): "Mis-trained branch predictions for return instructions may allow arbitrary speculative code execution under certain microarchitecture-dependent conditions." CVE-2022-29901 (published 2022-07-12): "Intel microprocessor generations 6 to 8 are affected by a new Spectre variant that is able to bypass their retpoline mitigation in the kernel to leak arbitrary data." (Both are known as Retbleed.) [CVE-2022-29900](https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2022-29900) · [CVE-2022-29901](https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2022-29901)
- **ISA support for constant-time code (primary, RISC-V unprivileged manual 20260120, scalar cryptography chapter, read 20 Nov 2026):** the Zkt subset "allows CPU implementers to indicate to cryptographic software developers that a subset of RISC-V instructions are guaranteed to be implemented such that their execution latency is independent of the data values they operate on." [Scalar cryptography](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/unpriv/scalar-crypto.html)

## R-215 · RISC-V privileged ISA: virtual memory and traps

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 from the privileged volume of the ratified manual set 20260120 (Supervisor ISA 1.13, Machine ISA 1.13; see R-201) on docs.riscv.org (primary); tagged [Established]. The Sv32 bit layouts come from the spec's SVG figures ("Sv32 virtual address", "Sv32 page table entry", satp for SXLEN = 32), whose labels were read directly.*

- **Sv32:** "Sv32 implementations support a 32-bit virtual address space, divided into pages"; "The 20-bit VPN is translated into a 22-bit physical page number (PPN), while the 12-bit page offset is untranslated"; translation uses "a two-level page table"; "Sv32 page tables consist of 2^10 page-table entries (PTEs), each of four bytes. A page table is exactly the size of a page and must always be aligned to a page boundary. The physical page number of the root page table is stored in the satp register." "Any level of PTE may be a leaf PTE, so in addition to 4 KiB pages, Sv32 supports 4 MiB megapages." Virtual address: VPN[1] bits 31–22, VPN[0] bits 21–12, page offset bits 11–0. PTE: PPN[1] bits 31–20 (12 bits), PPN[0] bits 19–10, RSW bits 9–8, then D, A, G, U, X, W, R, V in bits 7–0; "When all three are zero, the PTE is a pointer to the next level of the page table; otherwise, it is a leaf PTE." [Supervisor chapter](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/priv/supervisor.html)
- **Translation algorithm (§11.1.3.2):** start at satp.ppn × PAGESIZE with i = LEVELS − 1 (Sv32: PAGESIZE = 2^12, LEVELS = 2, PTESIZE = 4); read the PTE at a + va.vpn[i] × PTESIZE; fault if V = 0 or (R = 0 and W = 1); a PTE with R or X set is a leaf, otherwise descend; a leaf above level 0 with nonzero low PPN bits is a misaligned superpage (page fault); check U against the privilege mode, then R/W/X; set A (and D for stores) or fault (Svade); pa.pgoff = va.pgoff, and for a superpage the low PPN fields come from the VPN.
- **Larger modes:** Sv39 translates a 27-bit VPN to a 44-bit PPN "via a three-level page table" with 2 MiB megapages and 1 GiB gigapages; Sv48 uses four levels (adding 512 GiB terapages); Sv57 adds a fifth: "in addition to 4 KiB pages, Sv57 supports 2 MiB megapages, 1 GiB gigapages, 512 GiB terapages, and 256 TiB petapages" (read 20 Nov 2026 for the Course 14 audit, [Supervisor-level ISA](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/priv/supervisor.html)). The 4 KiB base page was chosen deliberately: "After much deliberation, we have settled on a conventional page size of 4 KiB for both RV32 and RV64"; "The TLB reach problem is ameliorated by transparent superpage support in modern operating systems."
- **satp and SFENCE.VMA:** satp (SXLEN = 32) holds MODE in bit 31, ASID in bits 30–22 and the root PPN in bits 21–0 ("We store the ASID and the page table base address in the same CSR to allow the pair to be changed atomically on a context switch"); SFENCE.VMA "is used to flush any local hardware caches related to address translation", and the remote-hart procedure (fence, interprocessor interrupt, remote SFENCE.VMA, acknowledgement) "is, of course, the RISC-V analog to a TLB shootdown".
- **Traps (machine chapter):** "When a trap is taken into M-mode, mepc is written with the virtual address of the instruction that was interrupted or that encountered the exception"; mtval holds exception-specific information or zero; in vectored mode, interrupts set pc to BASE + 4 × cause ("a machine-mode timer interrupt … causes the pc to be set to BASE+0x1c"). mcause exception codes: 8 environment call from U-mode, 9 from S-mode, 11 from M-mode, 12 instruction page fault, 13 load page fault, 15 store/AMO page fault; interrupt codes: 1/3 supervisor/machine software, 5/7 supervisor/machine timer, 9/11 supervisor/machine external. xRET restores the privilege mode from xPP and the interrupt enable from xPIE. [Machine chapter](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/priv/machine.html)

## R-216 · PCI Express generations 1.0–8.0

*Read on 20 Nov 2026. pcisig.com and businesswire.com returned Cloudflare/Akamai 403s, so PCI-SIG's releases for 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 were read as verbatim trade-press reprints (secondary copies), and the history of 1.0–5.0 from an article by a PCI-SIG board member (secondary, expert). Tagged [Established] for rates and encodings.*

- **Generations 1.0–5.0** (D. Das Sharma, PCI-SIG Board Member and Intel Fellow, "What's the Difference Going from PCIe 3.0 to PCIe 6.0?", *Electronic Design*): "PCIe 2.0 specification doubled the data rate to 5.0 GT/s in 2006. The first two generations of PCIe technology used 8b/10b encoding, incurring a 25% encoding overhead"; for PCIe 3.0, "a strategic decision was made to increase the data rate to 8.0 GT/s instead of 10.0 GT/s. This was augmented with a new 128b/130b encoding mechanism"; "October 2017: PCIe 4.0 Specification at 16.0 GT/s"; "May 2019: PCIe 5.0 Specification at 32.0 GT/s". [Electronic Design](https://www.electronicdesign.com/industrial-automation/article/21136215/whats-the-difference-going-from-pcie-30-to-pcie-60)
- **PCIe 6.0** (PCI-SIG release, January 2022; reprint dated 14 Jan 2022): "64 GT/s raw data rate and up to 256 GB/s via x16 configuration; Pulse Amplitude Modulation with four levels (PAM4) signaling…; Lightweight Forward Error Correct (FEC) and Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) mitigate the bit error rate increase associated with PAM4 signaling; Flit (flow control unit) based encoding". The original release date (believed 11 Jan 2022) was not confirmed. [Reprint](https://www.signalintegrityjournal.com/articles/2390-pci-sig-releases-pcie-60-specification-delivering-record-performance-to-power-big-data-applications)
- **PCIe 7.0** (released to members 11 Jun 2025; reprint dated 12 Jun 2025): "reaching 128.0 GT/s"; up to 512 GB/s bidirectional on x16; PAM4 and Flit encoding; "continues our long-standing tradition of doubling the IO bandwidth every three years" (Al Yanes, PCI-SIG). [Reprint](https://www.signalintegrityjournal.com/articles/3984-pci-sig-releases-pcie-70-specification-to-support-the-bandwidth-demands-of-artificial-intelligence-at-1280-gt-s-transfer-rates)
- **PCIe 8.0** (announced Aug 2025): target 256.0 GT/s, up to 1 TB/s bidirectional on x16, "planned for release to members by 2028". [Reprint](https://www.cotsjournalonline.com/pci-sig-announces-pci-express-8-0-specification-to-reach-256-0-gt-s/)
- **Derived:** PCI-SIG's x16 figures are bidirectional totals of the raw rate: 64 GT/s × 16 lanes × 2 directions / 8 = 256 GB/s, before Flit and FEC overhead.

## R-218 · RISC-V RVWMO, Ztso and atomics

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 from the unprivileged volume of the ratified manual set 20260120 on docs.riscv.org (primary; see R-201); tagged [Established].*

- **RVWMO (Chapter 17, "RVWMO Memory Consistency Model, Version 2.0"):** "Under RVWMO, code running on a single hart appears to execute in order from the perspective of other memory instructions in the same hart, but memory instructions from another hart may observe the memory instructions from the first hart being executed in a different order. Therefore, multithreaded code may require explicit synchronization to guarantee ordering between memory instructions from different harts. The base RISC-V ISA provides a FENCE instruction for this purpose"; "The RVWMO memory model is defined in terms of the global memory order, a total ordering of the memory operations produced by all harts." [RVWMO](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/unpriv/rvwmo.html)
- **Ztso:** the manual's table of contents lists Chapter 18, "'Ztso' Extension for Total Store Ordering, Version 1.0".
- **Same-address ordering:** the explanatory chapter notes that RVWMO enforces "CoRR (Coherence for Read-Read pairs)", part of "sequential consistency per location". [Explanatory material](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/unpriv/mm-eplan.html)
- **A extension:** "LR.W loads a word from the address in rs1, places the sign-extended value in rd, and registers a reservation set"; "SC.W conditionally writes a word in rs2 to the address in rs1: the SC.W succeeds only if the reservation is still valid and the reservation set contains the bytes being written. If the SC.W succeeds, the instruction writes the word in rs2 to memory, and it writes zero to rd. If the SC.W fails, the instruction does not write to memory, and it writes a nonzero value to rd." "The A extension comprises instructions provided by the Zaamo and Zalrsc extensions." §12.1.3, "Eventual Success of Store-Conditional Instructions": "The Zalrsc extension defines constrained LR/SC loops", which "must comprise at most 16 instructions placed sequentially in memory", with only base-I instructions (no loads, stores or backward jumps) between the LR and the SC. [A extension](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/unpriv/a-st-ext.html) The guarantee (read 20 Nov 2026 for the Course 14 audit): "If a hart H enters a constrained LR/SC loop, the execution environment must guarantee that one of the following events eventually occurs: H or some other hart executes a successful SC to the reservation set …; some other hart executes an unconditional store or AMO …; H executes a branch or jump that exits the constrained LR/SC loop; H traps." The commentary calls it "an architectural guarantee of livelock freedom" and notes "Earlier versions of this specification imposed a stronger starvation-freedom guarantee."

## R-219 · x86-TSO (Sewell et al., CACM 2010)

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 from the authors' final version of the CACM Research Highlights paper (dated 17 May 2010) on the Cambridge weak-memory pages (primary, author copy); tagged [Established].*

- P. Sewell, S. Sarkar, S. Owens, F. Zappa Nardelli and M. O. Myreen, "x86-TSO: A Rigorous and Usable Programmer's Model for x86 Multiprocessors", *Communications of the ACM* 53(7), July 2010. [Author version (PDF)](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~pes20/weakmemory/cacm.pdf)
- **SB:** for x86, with x and y initially 0, "if two processors respectively write 1 to x and y and then read from y and x …, it is possible for both to read 0 in the same execution … this result cannot arise from any interleaving"; "Allowed Final State: Proc 0:EAX=0 ∧ Proc 1:EBX=0"; explained "as a visible consequence of store buffering".
- **The model:** shared memory, "a global lock to indicate when a particular hardware thread has exclusive access to memory, and one store buffer per hardware thread"; "The store buffers are FIFO and a reading thread must read its most recent buffered write, if there is one, to that address; otherwise reads are satisfied from shared memory"; "An MFENCE instruction flushes the store buffer of that thread"; a LOCK'd instruction takes the global lock and flushes the buffer at its end.

## R-220 · NVIDIA H100 (Hopper) specifications

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by this session's fact-finding pass (quotes recorded verbatim at the time): the product page and the Hopper blog are primary; the architecture whitepaper (V1.02) was read only as a third-party mirror and carries preliminary figures, so its performance numbers are not used. Tagged [Established] as vendor specifications.*

- **Product page, H100 SXM** ("Product Specifications"): FP64 34 TFLOPS; FP64 Tensor 67; FP32 67; TF32 Tensor 989*; BF16 and FP16 Tensor 1,979*; FP8 Tensor 3,958*; INT8 3,958 TOPS*; "GPU Memory 80GB"; "GPU Memory Bandwidth 3.35TB/s"; "Max Thermal Design Power (TDP) Up to 700W (configurable)"; NVLink 900 GB/s; PCIe Gen5 128 GB/s; footnote "* With sparsity". [NVIDIA H100](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/)
- **Hopper blog** (NVIDIA Technical Blog, "NVIDIA Hopper Architecture In-Depth", 22 Mar 2022): H100 SXM5 has "8 GPCs, 66 TPCs, 2 SMs/TPC, 132 SMs per GPU; 128 FP32 CUDA Cores per SM, 16896 FP32 CUDA Cores per GPU; 4 fourth-generation Tensor Cores per SM, 528 per GPU; 80 GB HBM3, 5 HBM3 stacks, 10 512-bit memory controllers; 50 MB L2 cache"; each SM has 256 KB of combined L1 cache and shared memory; GH100 is built on TSMC 4N with 80 billion transistors on 814 mm²; "The Sparsity feature exploits fine-grained structured sparsity in deep learning networks, doubling the performance of standard Tensor Core operations." [Hopper In-Depth](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-hopper-architecture-in-depth/)
- **Thread-block clusters (Hopper blog, read 20 Nov 2026 for the Course 14 audit):** "Clusters enable multiple thread blocks running concurrently across multiple SMs to synchronize and collaboratively fetch and exchange data." "With clusters, it is possible for all the threads to directly access other SM's shared memory with load, store, and atomic operations. This feature is called distributed shared memory (DSMEM)."
- **Derived (not stated by NVIDIA):** dense BF16/FP16 Tensor ≈ 989.5 TFLOPS (half the sparse figure); the FP32 rate implies a boost clock of about 67 × 10¹² / (16,896 × 2) ≈ 1.98 GHz. NVIDIA's product page states no clock.

- **GB200 NVL72** (specifications table): a GB200 superchip (1 Grace CPU, 2 Blackwell GPUs) lists NVFP4 Tensor 40 PFLOPS sparse / 20 dense, FP8/FP6 20 PFLOPS and FP16/BF16 10 PFLOPS (sparse; "Dense is one-half sparse spec shown"), and HBM3E "372 GB, 16 TB/s"; the 72-GPU rack has 13.4 TB of HBM3E at 576 TB/s. [GB200 NVL72](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/gb200-nvl72/)
- **DGX B200** (8 Blackwell GPUs): 1,440 GB of HBM3e at 64 TB/s in total; FP4 Tensor 144 PFLOPS sparse / 72 dense; maximum system power about 14.3 kW. [DGX B200](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/dgx-b200/)
- **Derived per GPU:** from the rack, 13.4 TB / 72 ≈ 186 GB and 576 / 72 = 8 TB/s; from DGX B200, 1,440 / 8 = 180 GB and 64 / 8 = 8 TB/s. The two capacity figures differ (186 against 180 GB), presumably by product configuration; the bandwidth agrees.
