- **TPU v4** (N. P. Jouppi et al., "TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings", ISCA 2023, doi:10.1145/3579371.3589350; [arXiv 2304.01433](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.01433)): "Each TC contains four 128x128 Matrix Multiply Units (MXUs) and a Vector Processing Unit (VPU) with 128 lanes (16 ALUs per lane) and a 16 MiB Vector Memory (VMEM)"; 2 TensorCores per chip; Table 4: "Peak TFLOPS 275 (bf16 or int8) | 123 (bf16)" for v4 against v3, "HBM2 capacity, BW 32 GiB, 1200 GB/s | 32 GiB, 900 GB/s"; clock 1050 MHz; 7 nm, under 600 mm², 22 billion transistors; 6 ICI links at 50 GB/s; systems of up to 4096 chips; first deployed 2020.

- **Derived:** 2 × 4 × 128 × 128 MACs × 2 FLOP × 1.05 GHz = 275.25 TFLOPS, matching the paper's 275.

[v6e](https://cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/v6e) · [TPU7x](https://cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/tpu7x)

## R-223 · SPEC CPU 2017 and SPEC CPU 2026

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by this session's fact-finding pass from spec.org (primary); tagged [Established].*

- **CPU 2017:** 43 benchmarks in four suites (SPECspeed 2017 Integer and Floating Point: time for one copy; SPECrate 2017 Integer and Floating Point: throughput of N concurrent copies). A benchmark's ratio is the reference machine's time over the system under test's time (multiplied by the number of copies for SPECrate); the overall metric is the geometric mean of the ratios; with three runs the median is used. Worked examples from the overview: "The reference machine ran 600.perlbench_s in 1775 seconds. … 1775/354.329738 = 5.009458"; "8*(1592/541.52471) = 23.518776". Base and peak: "The base metrics (such as SPECspeed2017_int_base) require that all modules of a given language in a suite must be compiled using the same flags, in the same order. All reported results must include the base metric. The optional peak metrics … allow greater flexibility. Different compiler options may be used for each benchmark, and feedback-directed optimization is allowed." [Overview](https://www.spec.org/cpu2017/Docs/overview.html)
- **Retirement and successor:** "With the release of SPEC CPU 2026, SPEC has retired SPEC CPU 2017 as of November 17, 2026." SPEC CPU 2026 was released on 5 May 2026; it "Includes 52 benchmarks, up from 43, with more than two times the lines of source code", from 38 applications; it keeps the SPECspeed/SPECrate and base/peak structure; SPECspeed Integer now has explicit parallelism and its memory requirement rose from 16 GB to 64 GB. [CPU 2017 page](https://www.spec.org/cpu2017/) · [Press release, 5 May 2026](https://www.spec.org/pressreleases/2026/20260505-spec-releases-cpu-2026-benchmark-suite/) · [CPU 2026 overview](https://www.spec.org/cpu2026/Docs/overview.html)

## R-224 · MLPerf divisions and scenarios

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by this session's fact-finding pass from MLCommons' rules on GitHub (primary; inference rules at commit d3eba2f, training rules at commit 14bc89f). The rules change every round; cite the commit and date.*

- **Inference:** "The Closed division requires using pre-processing, post-processing, and model that is equivalent to the reference or alternative implementation. The closed division allows calibration for quantization and does not allow any retraining." "The Open division allows using arbitrary pre- or post-processing and model, including retraining. The qualified name 'MLPerf Open' must be used when referring to an Open Division suite result". Scenarios: single stream (90th-percentile latency), multistream (99th-percentile latency), server/interactive (Poisson arrivals; maximum throughput under a latency bound) and offline (throughput). [Inference rules](https://github.com/mlcommons/inference_policies/blob/master/inference_rules.adoc)
- **Training:** "The Closed division requires using the same preprocessing, model, training method, and quality target as the reference implementation"; the Open division allows arbitrary data, preprocessing, model or method. The current closed-division table (labelled v6.1) lists FLUX.1, GPT_OSS_20B, Llama31_8b, Llama2_70B_LoRA, deepseekv3_671b, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and dlrm_v4_hstu. [Training rules](https://github.com/mlcommons/training_policies/blob/master/training_rules.adoc)

## R-226 · Google's first TPU (Jouppi et al., ISCA 2017)

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 for the Course 14 audit from the authors' arXiv version (primary, author copy); tagged [Established].*

- **Matrix unit:** "The matrix unit holds one 64 KiB tile of weights plus one for double-buffering (to hide the 256 cycles it takes to shift a tile in)." "Figure 4 shows that data flows in from the left, and the weights are loaded from the top." "The weights are preloaded, and take effect with the advancing wave alongside the first data of a new block."

- **Sparsity:** "This unit is designed for dense matrices. Sparse architectural support was omitted for time-to-deploy reasons."

## R-231 · Linux power-allocator thermal governor (PID form and defaults)

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 from the kernel source tree, `Documentation/driver-api/thermal/power_allocator.rst` on the master branch of the Linux repository on GitHub (primary); tagged [Established].*

- "The power allocator governor implements a Proportional-Integral-Derivative controller (PID controller) with temperature as the control input and power as the controlled output: P_max = k_p * e + k_i * err_integral + k_d * diff_err + sustainable_power", with e = desired_temperature − current_temperature. [power_allocator.rst](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/Documentation/driver-api/thermal/power_allocator.rst)
- Two proportional constants: `k_po` during temperature overshoot (above the desired temperature) and `k_pu` during undershoot. Defaults: k_pu = 2 × sustainable_power/(desired_temperature − switch_on_temp); k_po = sustainable_power/(desired_temperature − switch_on_temp).
- "Typically `k_i` is set low (1 or 2) and `integral_cutoff` is 0"; for `k_d`, "It's recommended to leave it as the default: 0."
- "For reference, the sustainable power of a 4" phone is typically 2000mW, while on a 10" tablet is around 4500mW (may vary depending on screen size)."
- Perishable: kernel documentation changes between releases; recheck the current file before quoting defaults.

## R-232 · ACPI 6.5/6.6 passive-cooling equations

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 from the UEFI Forum's HTML edition of the specification (primary); tagged [Established].*

- UEFI Forum, *Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) Specification*, version 6.5, chapter 11 (Thermal Management). [Chapter 11](https://uefi.org/specs/ACPI/6.5/11_Thermal_Management.html)
- §11.1.5.1 (Processor Clock Throttling), Equation #1: ΔP [%] = _TC1 × (T_n − T_(n−1)) + _TC2 × (T_n − T_t), where T_n is the current temperature and T_t the target (_PSV); "The two coefficients _TC1 and _TC2 and the sampling period _TSP are hardware-dependent constants the OEM must supply to OSPM."
- Equation #2: P_n = P_(n−1) + HW[−ΔP], with Minimum % ≤ P_n ≤ 100%; values outside the range are truncated; Minimum% is the _MTL limit (or 0%); HW maps to the next available frequency setting.
- §11.4.22 (_TSP): the sampling period is returned "in tenths of seconds"; "The granularity of the sampling period is 0.1 seconds." §11.4.17 (_TFP) gives an optional fast sampling period in milliseconds.
- Re-read 20 Nov 2026 for the Course 15 audit: version 6.6 (uefi.org/specs/ACPI/6.6/11_Thermal_Management.html) carries the same Equations #1 and #2 in §11.1.5.1 and the same `_TSP` text in §11.4.22. §11.4.17 `_TFP`: "The granularity of the sampling period is 1 milliseconds"; "If both _TFP and _TSP are present in a Thermal Zone, _TFP overrides _TSP." [ACPI 6.6, chapter 11](https://uefi.org/specs/ACPI/6.6/11_Thermal_Management.html)
- Perishable: check for a newer ACPI version before citing section numbers.

## R-234 · IEEE P802.3dj: status and electrical signaling

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 from IEEE 802.3 task-force documents and IEEE SA governance agendas (primary; fetched with curl through the build proxy by a research subagent). Tagged [Established]; the final draft text (members only) was not read.*

- **Status:** the third SA recirculation ballot on Draft 3.3 (25 Sep – 10 Oct 2026) returned 133 approve (97%) with 8 comments, "All out of scope" ([Nov 2026 task-force report](https://www.ieee802.org/3/minutes/nov26/1126_3dj_open_report.pdf)). The 8 Dec 2026 RevCom agenda lists "P802.3dj/Draft 3.3 IEEE Draft Standard for Ethernet Amendment 13", and the SASB meets 9 Dec 2026 ([RevCom agenda](https://standards.ieee.org/wp-content/uploads/import/governance/revcom/revcom-agenda.pdf); rolling URL). Not yet an approved standard as of 20 Nov 2026. The PAR (approved 3 Dec 2022) was recommended for extension to 31 Dec 2027 on 21 Sep 2026.
- **Electrical signaling:** key motion (May 2023): "Adopt differential PAM4 signaling as the basis for all of the 200 Gbps/lane passive copper cable and backplane PMDs and adopt RS(544,514,10) as the only FEC" ([key motions](https://www.ieee802.org/3/dj/projdoc/KeyMotions_3dj_240516.pdf)). Baseline proposal (Jan 2024): "Nominal signaling rate 106.25 GBd, PAM4 modulation" for chip-to-chip; "106.25 GBd ± 50 ppm" for 800GBASE-KR4 and 1.6TBASE-KR8 ([baseline](https://www.ieee802.org/3/dj/public/24_01/ran_3dj_01a_2401.pdf)).
- **Arithmetic (ours):** 106.25 GBd × 2 bit = 212.5 Gb/s = 200 × (257/256) × (544/514); its Nyquist frequency is the 53.125 GHz of the loss objectives (R-141). Optical inner-FEC lanes run at 113.4375 GBd (Table 174-6, per a Draft 3.1 comment); do not confuse the two.
- Perishable: re-check approval after the 9 Dec 2026 SASB meeting.

## R-236 · OFDM numerology: 802.11a/g, LTE and 5G NR cyclic prefixes

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent: 3GPP specifications as published by ETSI (primary), an IEEE 802.11 working-group document (the published IEEE Std 802.11 now requires a sign-in and was not opened), cross-checked against ETSI HIPERLAN/2, Keysight and MathWorks documentation. Tagged [Established]; quotations as the subagent recorded them; values marked derived are arithmetic from the quoted ones.*

- **802.11a/g, 20 MHz** (IEEE 802.11 doc. 11-05/1102r4, Table 1, legacy column; ETSI TS 101 475 V1.3.1 Table 6 for the identical HIPERLAN/2 numerology; MathWorks `wlanNonHTOFDMInfo`): 64 subcarriers at 20 MHz, "312.5kHz (20MHz/64)"; 48 data and 4 pilot subcarriers (52 used); "TFFT: IFFT/FFT period 3.2µsec"; "TGI: Guard Interval length 0.8µsec= TFFT/4" (16 samples; `CPLength: 16`); "TSYM: Symbol Interval 4µsec". 802.11n: "TGIS: Short Guard Interval length 0.4µsec= TFFT/8", optional on transmit and receive. Derived: prefix overhead 16/80 = 20%. [11-05/1102r4](https://mentor.ieee.org/802.11/dcn/05/11-05-1102-04-000n-joint-proposal-phy-specification.doc); [ETSI TS 101 475](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/101400_101499/101475/01.03.01_60/ts_101475v010301p.pdf)
- **LTE** (ETSI TS 136 211 V19.3.0 = 3GPP TS 36.211 Rel-19): "Ts = 1/(15000 × 2048) seconds"; N = 2048 for Δf = 15 kHz; Table 6.12-1 normal cyclic prefix "160 for l = 0", "144 for l = 1,2,...,6"; extended 512; "Tslot = 15360 · Ts = 0.5 ms". Derived: 30.72 MHz sampling, 66.67 µs useful symbol, 5.208 and 4.6875 µs prefixes, prefix overhead (160 + 6 × 144)/15360 = 6.67%. [TS 136 211](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/136200_136299/136211/19.03.00_60/ts_136211v190300p.pdf)
- **5G NR** (ETSI TS 138 211 V19.5.0 = 3GPP TS 38.211 Rel-19): Tc = 1/(Δfmax·Nf), Δfmax = 480 kHz, Nf = 4096, κ = Ts/Tc = 64; Table 4.2-1: Δf = 2^μ·15 kHz for μ = 0..6, extended cyclic prefix only for μ = 2; clause 5.3.1: useful part 2048κ·2^−μ, normal prefix 144κ·2^−μ (plus 16κ for l = 0 or 7·2^μ), extended 512κ·2^−μ, in units of Tc. Derived: normal prefix 4.6875 µs at μ = 0, 0.293 µs at μ = 4 (240 kHz), 0.073 µs at μ = 6. [TS 138 211](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/138200_138299/138211/19.05.00_60/ts_138211v190500p.pdf)
- Not confirmed: the clause and table numbers of the timing table in the current IEEE Std 802.11; the claim that 240 kHz spacing is used only for synchronization blocks.

## R-237 · ADC dynamic testing: IEEE 1241, ENOB conventions, coherent sampling, a data-sheet example

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent (curl through the build proxy): the IEEE SA standard pages, TI documents and data sheet, a Renesas application note and a Rohde & Schwarz technical paper. The text of IEEE 1241 itself was not opened (paywalled), so its ENOB definition is reported second-hand. analog.com refused automated access and was not used. Quotations as the subagent recorded them.*

- **IEEE Std 1241-2023** ("Standard for Terminology and Test Methods for Analog-to-Digital Converters") is the active edition: Board approval 2023-06-05, published 2023-10-06, superseding 1241-2010 (now "Inactive-Reserved"). No revision project was listed in Nov 2026. [Established] [IEEE SA 1241-2023](https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/1241/6797/)
- **ENOB, SINAD form:** TI *Analog Engineer's Pocket Reference* (SLYW038D, rev. Apr 2025): "ENOB = (SINAD(dB) − 1.76 dB) / 6.02", with SINAD defined relative to "the RMS equivalent of the ADC's full-scale input" (full-scale-referred). [Established] [TI SLYW038D](https://www.ti.com/document-viewer/lit/html/SLYW038D/GUID-62961252-5D9A-4098-A630-21BD49A27DB2)
- **ENOB, IEEE 1241 form (second-hand):** Rohde & Schwarz technical paper 1ER03_1e (2011), citing IEEE 1241-2010: ENOB = 0.5·log2(SINAD) − 0.5·log2(1.5) − log2(A/V), with A the fitted sine's peak-to-peak amplitude and V the full-scale range; "any input amplitude can be used, since the difference between the full-scale amplitude and the actual test amplitude is taken into account". Derived (ours): this equals (SINAD_dBFS − 1.76)/6.02, the TI form. [R&S 1ER03_1e (PDF)](https://scdn.rohde-schwarz.com/ur/pws/dl_downloads/dl_application/application_notes/1er03/ENOB_Technical_Paper_1ER03_1e.pdf)
- **Coherent sampling:** TI SLVAG04 (R. ## R-241 · Arm CMSIS-DSP biquad cascade functions and conventions

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent from the official documentation site (footer "Generated on Thu Sep 10 2026 … for CMSIS-DSP 1.18.0"). The coefficient-negation sentence was re-read by the main author from the saved page.*

- Function families: Direct Form I `arm_biquad_cascade_df1_{f16,f32,q15,q31}` (plus `_fast_q15`, `_fast_q31`); Direct Form II transposed `arm_biquad_cascade_df2T_{f16,f32,f64}` and stereo variants; "Only floating-point data is supported" for DF2T. [Established] [CMSIS-DSP Biquad DF1](https://arm-software.github.io/CMSIS-DSP/latest/group__BiquadCascadeDF1.html), [DF2T](https://arm-software.github.io/CMSIS-DSP/latest/group__BiquadCascadeDF2T.html)
- Difference equation: "y[n] = b0 * x[n] + b1 * x[n-1] + b2 * x[n-2] + a1 * y[n-1] + a2 * y[n-2]"; "Some design tools use the difference equation … - a1 * y[n-1] - a2 * y[n-2]. In this case the feedback coefficients a1 and a2 must be negated when used with the CMSIS DSP Library." Coefficients stored per stage as {b0, b1, b2, a1, a2} (Q15 adds a zero after b0 for SIMD). [Established]
- Fixed point: "coefficients are restricted to lie in the range [-1 +1). The fixed-point functions have an additional scaling parameter postShift … This essentially scales the filter coefficients by 2^postShift"; Direct Form I "is numerically more robust for fixed-point data types… transposed Direct Form II … requires a wide dynamic range for the state variables." [Established]
- **Accumulator and scaling statements, from the source-file doc comments** (added 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent; `ARM-software/CMSIS-DSP`, branch `main` at commit 9f64ba31591e527c505951943b4b95b0eb2f834b, identical at tag v1.18.0; `Source/FilteringFunctions/`, file headers dated 23 April 2021, V1.9.0):
  - `arm_biquad_cascade_df1_q15.c`: "The 2.30 intermediate results are accumulated in a 64-bit accumulator in 34.30 format. There is no risk of internal overflow with this approach and the full precision of intermediate multiplications is preserved."
  - `arm_biquad_cascade_df1_q31.c`: "The function is implemented using an internal 64-bit accumulator. The accumulator has a 2.62 format and maintains full precision of the intermediate multiplication results but provides only a single guard bit. Thus, if the accumulator result overflows it wraps around rather than clip"; the input "must be scaled down by 2 bits and lie in the range [-0.25 +0.25)".
  - `arm_biquad_cascade_df1_fast_q15.c`: a "32-bit accumulator with 2.30 format" that "provides only a single guard bit"; `arm_biquad_cascade_df1_fast_q31.c`: products "truncated to 2.30 format" and "added to a 2.30 accumulator", with the same [−0.25, +0.25) input requirement. [Established] [Source files](https://github.com/ARM-software/CMSIS-DSP/tree/9f64ba31591e527c505951943b4b95b0eb2f834b/Source/FilteringFunctions)
- Perishable: library versions and function sets change.

- **TI SPRUIP0**, "C71x DSP CPU, Instruction Set, and Matrix Multiply Accelerator" (May 2021): "The first implementation of the C7x platform is a full-feature with 512-bit vector width CPU core"; "Dual data path with one 64-bit scalar side (Side A) and one 512-bit vector side (Side B)"; "traditional C6x VLIW DSP operating mode"; Table 3-1 (C7x vector side against C66x): fixed-point 16 × 16 MACs per cycle 32 → 128, 32 × 32 8 → 32, single-precision floating-point MACs 8 → 32, vector size 128 → 512 bits. MMA: "For 8-bit operands, there are 64 elements in row vector A and 4096 elements in square matrix B, resulting in a requirement for 4096 multiplications and the equivalent of 4096 summations per clock cycle" (1024 for 16-bit, 256 for 32-bit operands). [Established] [SPRUIP0](https://www.ti.com/lit/pdf/spruip0)
- **TI TDA4VM** data sheet SPRSP36L (revised June 2026): "C7x floating point, vector DSP, up to 1.0GHz, 80 GFLOPS, 256 GOPS"; "Deep-learning matrix multiply accelerator (MMA), up to 8 TOPS (8b) at 1.0GHz". Derived (ours): 128 × 2 × 1 GHz = 256 GOPS and 4096 × 2 × 1 GHz = 8.19 TOPS, consistent with both. TI's C7000 optimization guide (v4.1, 2024) calls the core "Very-Long-Instruction-Word (VLIW)". Smaller parts (AM62A7, TDA4AEN-Q1) use a 256-bit vector C7x at "up to 40 GFLOPS". [Established] [TDA4VM data sheet](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/tda4vm.pdf)

## R-257 · Spectrum-analyzer noise measurement (Keysight UXA, R&S FSW) and the kT0 reference

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent from the documents themselves (curl and pdftotext). Keysight's application notes AN 150 and AN 57-1 are now behind a registration form and were not read; MathWorks documentation refused automated access.*

- **Keysight N9041B UXA Signal Analyzer Specifications Guide** (N9041-90004, Edition 1, Feb 2024): resolution-filter "Noise BW to RBW ratio 1.056 ±2% (nominal)"; "The noise marker, band power marker, channel power and ACP all compute their results using the power bandwidth of the RBW used for the measurement"; "DANL is, by Keysight and industry practice, specified with log averaging, which reduces the measured noise level by 2.51 dB ... noise bandwidth of 1.056 Hz. Therefore, the noise density is 2.27 dB above the DANL"; in its noise-figure formula, kTB is "−173.98 dBm in a 1 Hz bandwidth at 290 K". (One footnote elsewhere in the same guide gives 2.25 dB, inconsistent with 2.51 − 0.24 = 2.27; the main text's 2.27 is used.) [Established] [UXA specifications](https://www.keysight.com/us/en/assets/9018-05001/technical-specifications/9018-05001.pdf)
- **Rohde & Schwarz FSW User Manual** (1173.9411.02, version 57, 2026), §8.3.4.2 "Measuring noise density": "Noise density is the noise referred to a bandwidth of 1 Hz"; the correction is "10 x lg (1 Hz/BWNoise)" with BWNoise the noise bandwidth of the RBW filter; with the RMS detector "With the exception of bandwidth correction, no further corrections are required"; with the sample detector "1.05 dB is added to the marker level. This is the difference between the average value and the RMS value of white noise", and "With a logarithmic level axis, 1.45 dB is added additionally"; with the RMS detector, trace averaging "produces noise levels that are too low and cannot be corrected"; a narrow logarithmic video bandwidth gives "a too low indication of the power (-2.51 dB at very low video bandwidths)". [Established] [FSW manual](https://scdn.rohde-schwarz.com/ur/pws/dl_downloads/pdm/cl_manuals/user_manual/1173_9411_01/FSW_UserManual_en_57.pdf)
- **Keysight 89600 VSA help, "Noise Measurements"**: "Averaging a noise-like signal on a log scale can cause an error as great as -2.51 dB." [Established]
- **ITU-R P.372-18** (09/2026), §1.2.1: "T0 : reference temperature (K) taken as 290 K". CODATA: k = 1.380 649 × 10⁻²³ J/K, exact. Derived: kT0 = 4.0039 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz = −173.98 dBm/Hz. [Established] [ITU-R P.372-18](https://www.itu.int/dms_pubrec/itu-r/rec/p/R-REC-P.372-18-202609-I!!PDF-E.pdf)
- Derived (ours, checked in verify_17_01.py by simulation): the Rayleigh envelope's mean is √(π/4) of its rms (−1.049 dB); log-averaging an exponentially distributed power reads low by 10 log10(e)·γ = 2.507 dB; their difference, 1.458 dB, is the R&S 1.45 dB.

## R-258 · 3GPP NR adjacent channel leakage ratio (TS 38.104, TS 38.101-1)

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent from the 3GPP specification archives (zip files of the published versions). Values were cross-checked against the Release-15 versions, which agree.*

- **TS 38.104 V20.1.0 (2026-09), base station:** ACLR is "the ratio of the filtered mean power centred on the assigned channel frequency to the filtered mean power centred on an adjacent channel frequency"; FR1 conducted (Table 6.6.3.2-1): 45 dB at the first and second adjacent NR channels (38 dB for band n104); absolute basic limits (Table 6.6.3.2-2): −13 dBm/MHz (Category A wide area), −15 (Category B wide area), −25 (medium range), −32 (local area), applied "whichever is less stringent"; FR2 (Table 9.7.3.3-1): 28 dB at 24.25–33.4 GHz, 26 dB at 37–52.6 GHz, 24 dB at 52.6–71 GHz (the last not in Release 15). [Established] [38.104 archive](https://www.3gpp.org/ftp/Specs/archive/38_series/38.104/38104-k10.zip)
- **TS 38.101-1 V20.1.0 (2026-09), UE:** NR ACLR (Table 6.5.2.4.1-2): power class 1: 37 dB, 1.5: 31 dB, 2: 31 dB, 3: 30 dB (26 dB in n104), applying when the adjacent-channel power exceeds −50 dBm; UTRA ACLR1 33 dB and ACLR2 36 dB with a 3.84 MHz RRC (roll-off 0.22) filter; §6.5.2.4: the result "should be integrated over the measurement bandwidth in order to obtain the equivalent noise bandwidth of the measurement bandwidth." [Established] [38.101-1 archive](https://www.3gpp.org/ftp/Specs/archive/38_series/38.101-1/38101-1-k10.zip)

## R-260 · 3GPP NR reference sensitivity and its noise-figure assumptions

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent and re-checked against the local copies of the published specification archives (zip/docx).*

- **TR 38.817-02 V15.12.0, §7.2.1 (base station):** reference sensitivity follows $P_{\text{REFSENS}} = -174 + 10\log_{10}(\text{BW}) + \text{NF} + \text{IM} + \text{SNR}$, where "NF is BS noise figure, equal to 5 dB for Wide Area BS, 10 dB for Medium Range BS and 13 dB for Local Area BS" and "IM is the implementation margin, equal to 2dB"; SNR is the value "for which we reach 95% throughput". [Established]
- **TR 38.817-01 V16.4.0, §6.2 (UE):** "Sensitivity = -174dBm(kT) + 10*log(RX BW) + NF + SNR +IM – diversity gain"; SNR −1 dB; "If 2Rx is considered, the diversity gain is 3dB and the Implementation Margin (IM) uses 2.5dB"; for bands n77–n79 "the agreed NR values are 10.5dB, 10dB and 10dB". [Established] UE REFSENS itself (TS 38.101-1 V20.1.0, §7.3.2) requires throughput "≥ 95 % of the maximum throughput of the reference measurement channels" of Annex A.3.2; Table A.3.2.2-1 ("Fixed reference channel for receiver requirements (SCS 15 kHz, FDD, QPSK 1/3)") specifies QPSK, target coding rate 1/3 and "Maximum number of HARQ transmissions" 1 (re-read 21 Nov 2026 from the local copy of the 38.101-1 archive). [Established]
- **TS 38.104 V20.1.0 (2026-09), Table 7.2.2-1:** wide-area BS REFSENS −101.7 dBm for 5–15 MHz channels at 15 kHz with reference channel G-FR1-A1-1, which Table A.1-1 defines as 25 resource blocks, QPSK, code rate 1/3. [Established] [38.104 archive](https://www.3gpp.org/ftp/Specs/archive/38_series/38.104/38104-k10.zip)
- **TS 38.101-1 V20.1.0 (2026-09), Table 7.3.2-1b:** two-port REFSENS for n78: −95.8 + 10log10(NRB/52) dBm at 15 kHz, −96.1 + 10log10(NRB/24) at 30 kHz, −96.5 + 10log10(NRB/11) at 60 kHz; note 1: four receive ports are the baseline for this band (two-port values are adjusted by Table 7.3.2-2). Derived (ours): the TR 38.817-01 equation with NF 10 dB reproduces −95.79 dBm for 52 RB at 15 kHz. [Established] [38.101-1 archive](https://www.3gpp.org/ftp/Specs/archive/38_series/38.101-1/38101-1-k10.zip)

## R-263 · US FM broadcast rules (47 CFR Part 73)

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent from the eCFR point-in-time XML (as of 18 Nov 2026) and re-checked against the saved text.*

- **§ 73.310(a):** "frequency deviation of ±75kHz is defined as 100% modulation"; an FM broadcast channel is "A band of frequencies 200 kHz wide", from 88.1 MHz "in successive steps of 200 kHz to and including 107.9 MHz". **§ 73.201:** the band "between 88 MHz and 108 MHz ... is divided into 100 channels of 200 kHz each". [Established] [eCFR Part 73](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-73)
- **§ 73.317:** (b) emissions 120–240 kHz from the carrier "must be attenuated at least 25 dB below the level of the unmodulated carrier"; (e) "Preemphasis shall not be greater than the impedance-frequency characteristics of a series inductance resistance network having a time constant of 75 microseconds" (a ceiling, not a fixed value). [Established]
- **§ 73.322 (stereo):** "The pilot subcarrier at 19 kHz ±2 Hz, must frequency modulate the main carrier between the limits of 8 and 10 percent"; the stereophonic subcarrier is the second harmonic (38 kHz); "Double sideband, suppressed-carrier, amplitude modulation of the stereophonic subcarrier at 38 kHz must be used", suppressed "to a level less than 1% modulation"; its modulating signal is L − R; the subcarrier's baseband range is 23 kHz to 53 kHz. [Established]

## R-279 · 3GPP NR channel coding (TS 38.212)

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent from the 3GPP archive (38212-j40.zip) and the identical ETSI PDF (TS 138 212 V19.4.0), whose equations extract as text; key passages re-checked against the saved text on 21 Nov 2026.*

- **TS 38.212 V19.4.0 (2026-06), Release 19, clause 5.3, Tables 5.3-1 and 5.3-2:** UL-SCH, DL-SCH and PCH use LDPC; BCH and DCI use polar codes; UCI uses a block code or a polar code. [Established] [38.212 archive](https://www.3gpp.org/ftp/Specs/archive/38_series/38.212/38212-j40.zip)
- **Clause 5.1:** six CRC generator polynomials: gCRC24A(D) = D^24 + D^23 + D^18 + D^17 + D^14 + D^11 + D^10 + D^7 + D^6 + D^5 + D^4 + D^3 + D + 1; gCRC24B(D) = D^24 + D^23 + D^6 + D^5 + D + 1; gCRC24C(D) = D^24 + D^23 + D^21 + D^20 + D^17 + D^15 + D^13 + D^12 + D^8 + D^4 + D^2 + D + 1; gCRC16(D) = D^16 + D^12 + D^5 + 1; gCRC11(D) = D^11 + D^10 + D^9 + D^5 + 1; gCRC6(D) = D^6 + D^5 + 1. Clauses 6.2.1/7.2.1: UL-SCH and DL-SCH transport blocks use CRC24A "if A > 3824" and CRC16 otherwise; clause 5.2.2: each LDPC code block after segmentation gets a 24-bit CRC with gCRC24B; clauses 7.1.3 and 7.3.2: BCH and DCI use CRC24C; clause 6.3.1.2.1: polar-coded UCI uses CRC6 for 12 ≤ A ≤ 19 and CRC11 for A ≥ 20. [Established] [ETSI TS 138 212](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/138200_138299/138212/19.04.00_60/ts_138212v190400p.pdf)
- **Clauses 5.2.2 and 5.3.2, Table 5.3.2-1:** maximum code block Kcb = 8448 (base graph 1) and 3840 (base graph 2); codeword length N = 66·Zc (BG1) and 50·Zc (BG2); base matrices of 46 × 68 (BG1) and 42 × 52 (BG2), each 1 replaced by a Zc × Zc circularly shifted identity; lifting sizes in eight sets up to Zc = 384. Clause 6.2.2: base graph 2 "if A ≤ 292, or if A ≤ 3824 and R ≤ 0.67, or if R ≤ 0.25", otherwise base graph 1. Clause 5.3.1.2: polar sequence for Nmax = 1024. Derived (ours): 8448 = 22 × 384 and 3840 = 10 × 384; lowest mother-code rates 22/66 = 1/3 and 10/50 = 1/5. [Established]
- **Polar mother-code length by channel (ETSI TS 138 212 V19.4.0, 2026-07, re-read 21 Nov 2026 from the saved PDF):** clause 7.1.4 (BCH) and clause 7.3.3 (DCI) encode "via Polar coding according to Clause 5.3.1, by setting nmax = 9" (mother code N ≤ 512); clause 6.3.1.3 (UCI) sets "nmax = 10" (N ≤ 1024). [Established]

## R-280 · Ethernet "KP4" Reed–Solomon FEC, RS(544,514)

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent from public ieee802.org documents; the published IEEE 802.3 standard is paywalled and was not read. Re-checked against the saved text on 21 Nov 2026.*

- **IEEE Draft P802.3bs/D3.1 (30 Jan 2017), Clause 119 (200GBASE-R and 400GBASE-R PCS):** "The PCS shall implement an RS(544,514) based FEC encoder"; "α is a primitive element of the finite field defined by the polynomial x10+x3+1"; "The Reed-Solomon decoder shall be capable of correcting any combination of up to t=15 symbol errors in a codeword." [Established, draft text] [gustlin_3bs_03_0317](https://www.ieee802.org/3/bs/public/17_03/gustlin_3bs_03_0317.pdf)
- **Cideciyan, Gustlin, Li, Wang, Wang, "Next Generation Backplane and Copper Cable Challenges", *IEEE Communications Magazine*, Dec 2013:** the NRZ PHY (100GBASE-KR4/CR4) uses "an RS(528, 514, t = 7, m = 10) code", the PAM-4 PHY "an RS(544, 514, t = 15, m = 10) code". [Established] [copy on ieee802.org](https://www.ieee802.org/3/400GSG/email/pdf7vtAkT89g3.pdf)
- **Gustlin and Lusted, "802.3bj FEC Overview and Status", IEEE P802.3db task force ad hoc (June 2020, from the file name):** 802.3bj defines both RS(528,514) and RS(544,514); 802.3bs uses RS(544,514) (Clause 119); 802.3cd, 802.3ck and 802.3cu require RS(544,514); "RS(544,514) used for 50/100G per lane technology / RS(528,514) is used for 25G technology"; RS(544,514) is "aka 'KP4'". [Established, secondary (task-force slides)] [gustlin_3db_adhoc_01_062520](https://www.ieee802.org/3/db/public/adhoc/presentations/gustlin_3db_adhoc_01_062520.pdf)

## R-281 · The rate-1/2, K = 7 convolutional code (CCSDS; 802.11)

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent; re-checked against the saved CCSDS text on 21 Nov 2026. The IEEE 802.11 text is paywalled and was not read.*

- **CCSDS 131.0-B-5, "TM Synchronization and Channel Coding", Blue Book, Sept 2023, §3.3.1:** "The basic convolutional code shall be the non-systematic code with the following characteristics: (1) Nomenclature: Convolutional code with maximum-likelihood decoding. (2) Code rate (r): 1/2 bit per symbol. (3) Constraint length (K): 7 bits. (4) Connection vectors: G1 = 1111001 (171 octal); G2 = 1011011 (133 octal). (5) Symbol inversion: On output path of G2." The same vectors define the punctured codes of §3.4. [Established] [CCSDS 131.0-B-5](https://ccsds.org/Pubs/131x0b5.pdf)
- **Yan and Dai, arXiv:2502.15475 (2025), §2.1.1:** IEEE 802.11's convolutional encoder has generators g0 = 133₈ and g1 = 171₈, "a mother code rate of 1/2 and a constraint length of 7", punctured to rates 2/3, 3/4 and 5/6. The output ordering in the 802.11 text itself was not verified. [Established, secondary] [arXiv:2502.15475](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.15475)
- **CCSDS 131.0-B-5, table of contents (saved text, re-read 21 Nov 2026):** besides the convolutional and Reed–Solomon codes, the Blue Book specifies turbo coding (section 6) and LDPC coding of a transfer frame (section 7: a rate-223/255 code, §7.3, and a family with rates 1/2, 2/3 and 4/5, §7.4) and of a stream of sync-marked frames (section 8). [Established]

## R-282 · ITU-R P.525-5 free-space attenuation

*Read on 20 Nov 2026 by a research subagent from the ITU PDF; re-checked against the saved text on 21 Nov 2026.*

- **Recommendation ITU-R P.525-5 (11/2024), "Calculation of free-space attenuation"**, in force, superseding P.525-4 (08/2019). Annex 1, eq. (5): $L_{bf} = 20\log_{10}(4\pi d/\lambda)$ dB with $d$ and λ in the same unit; eq. (6): "$L_{bf}$ = 32.4 + 20 log10 f + 20 log10 d dB" with f in MHz and d in km. Derived (ours): the exact constant is $20\log_{10}(4\pi \times 10^9/c)$ = 32.45 dB. [Established] [P.525-5](https://www.itu.int/dms_pubrec/itu-r/rec/p/R-REC-P.525-5-202411-I!!PDF-E.pdf)

## R-286 · NR OFDM symbol and cyclic-prefix timing (TS 38.211)

*Read on 21 Nov 2026 from the ETSI PDF of TS 38.211 V19.5.0 saved by a research subagent (its equations extract as text).*

- **TS 38.211 V19.5.0 (2026-09), clause 4.1:** "time units Tc = 1/(Δfmax · Nf) where Δfmax = 480·10³ Hz and Nf = 4096. The constant κ = Ts/Tc = 64 where Ts = 1/(Δfref · Nf,ref), Δfref = 15·10³ Hz and Nf,ref = 2048." **Clause 5.3.1:** useful symbol $N_u^\mu = 2048\kappa \cdot 2^{-\mu}$; cyclic prefix $N_{CP,l}^\mu = 512\kappa \cdot 2^{-\mu}$ (extended), $144\kappa \cdot 2^{-\mu} + 16\kappa$ (normal, $l = 0$ or $l = 7 \cdot 2^\mu$) and $144\kappa \cdot 2^{-\mu}$ (normal, other $l$), in units of $T_c$. **Clause 6.3.1.4 "Transform precoding"**: applied to the uplink when enabled (per TS 38.214), with a single layer. Derived (ours): $T = 1/\Delta f$; normal CP = 144/2048 of $T$ (4.69 μs at 15 kHz, 2.34 μs at 30 kHz); each subframe sums to exactly 1 ms. [Established] [ETSI TS 138 211](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/138200_138299/138211/19.05.00_60/ts_138211v190500p.pdf)

## R-292 · Ethernet framing (RFC 894; IEEE 802.3 interpretation)

*Read on 21 Nov 2026 with curl from rfc-editor.org and ieee802.org; the IEEE 802.3 standard itself is paywalled and was not read.*

- **RFC 894 (1984), "A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over Ethernet Networks":** Ethernet with "48-bit addresses"; "The minimum length of the data field of a packet sent over an Ethernet is 46 octets", padded with zeros if necessary; "the maximum length of an IP datagram sent over an Ethernet is 1500 octets" (the preceding sentence in the RFC says "minimum" where "maximum" is meant). [Established] [RFC 894](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc894.txt)
- **IEEE 802.3 interpretation request 1-11/09:** the committee's response states "The 96 bit value defined in sub clause 4.4.2 therefore applies at MAC transmit"; the request's own accounting uses "1518:data+8:preamble+12:IPG" bytes per maximum-size frame. Derived (ours): 1518 = 14-byte header + 1500 payload + 4-byte FCS; minimum frame 64 bytes = 14 + 46 + 4. [Established] [IEEE 802.3 interp 1-11/09](https://www.ieee802.org/3/interp/interp-1-1109.pdf)

## R-293 · IP, UDP, TCP, ARP, addressing and TLS (IETF RFCs)

*Read on 21 Nov 2026 with curl from rfc-editor.org.*

- **RFC 791 (IPv4):** Total Length allows datagrams "up to 65,535 octets"; all hosts must accept datagrams "of up to 576 octets"; Time to Live bounds a datagram's lifetime. **RFC 768 (UDP):** "Length is the length in octets of this user datagram including this header" (8-byte header: ports, length, checksum). **RFC 9293 (TCP, 2022):** 4-bit Data Offset (header length in 32-bit words; 20-byte minimum header), 16-bit Window field, "the three-way (or three message) handshake". **RFC 826:** Address Resolution Protocol. **RFC 1918:** private ranges "10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255 (10/8 prefix)", "172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255 (172.16/12 prefix)", "192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255 (192.168/16 prefix)". **RFC 4632:** CIDR. **RFC 8200 (IPv6):** 128-bit source and destination addresses, Hop Limit and Flow Label fields (40-byte fixed header), and every link "must be configured to have an MTU of at least 1280 octets". **RFC 2453 (RIP v2):** a metric of 16 "is normally referred to as 'infinity'". **RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3):** full handshake in one round trip, with an optional 0-RTT mode and its replay caveats. [Established] [RFC index](https://www.rfc-editor.org/)

## R-294 · TCP congestion control, timers and window scaling

*Read on 21 Nov 2026 with curl from rfc-editor.org.*

- **RFC 5681:** initial window "IW = 2 * SMSS bytes and MUST NOT be more than 2 segments" if SMSS > 2190 bytes, 3 segments if 1095 < SMSS ≤ 2190, 4 if SMSS ≤ 1095; slow start and congestion avoidance with "cwnd += SMSS*SMSS/cwnd" per ACK; slow-start threshold. **RFC 6298:** first measurement "SRTT <- R, RTTVAR <- R/2"; then "RTTVAR <- (1 - beta) * RTTVAR + beta * |SRTT - R'|", "SRTT <- (1 - alpha) * SRTT + alpha * R'", "RTO <- SRTT + max (G, K*RTTVAR)" with K = 4, "alpha=1/8 and beta=1/4"; "(2.4) Whenever RTO is computed, if it is less than 1 second, then the RTO SHOULD be rounded up to 1 second." **RFC 7323:** Window Scale option shift.cnt; "the shift count MUST be limited to 14 (which allows windows of 2^30 = 1 GiB)". [Established] [RFC 5681](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5681.txt), [RFC 6298](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6298.txt), [RFC 7323](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7323.txt)

## R-296 · TCP congestion control in practice: CUBIC, the initial window and timeout behaviour

*Read on 21 Nov 2026 from the RFC Editor's plain-text copies (rfc-editor.org), primary.*

- **RFC 9438, "CUBIC for Fast and Long-Distance Networks" (Standards Track, August 2023):** "CUBIC has been adopted as the default TCP congestion control algorithm by the Linux, Windows, and Apple stacks"; it "sets the multiplicative window decrease factor to 0.7, whereas Reno" uses 0.5, and "The parameter β_cubic SHOULD be set to 0.7". [Established]
- **RFC 6928, "Increasing TCP's Initial Window" (Experimental, April 2013):** raises the initial window "to 10 segments (maximum 14600 B)", specified as "min (10*MSS, max (2*MSS, 14600))". [Established]
- **RFC 5681 §3.1:** after a retransmission timeout, "ssthresh = max (FlightSize / 2, 2*SMSS)" and cwnd is set to "no more than the loss window, LW, which equals 1 full-sized segment". [Established]
- **RFC 6298:** "(5.5) The host MUST set RTO <- RTO * 2 ("back off the timer")"; "TCP MUST use Karn's algorithm [KP87] for taking RTT samples. That is, RTT samples MUST NOT be made using segments that were retransmitted". [Established]

## R-298 · Cortex-M interrupt latency

*Read on 21 Nov 2026 by a research subagent from Arm technical reference manuals.*

- **Cortex-M3 TRM DDI0337H and Cortex-M4 TRM DDI0439B:** "There is a maximum of a 12 cycle latency from asserting the interrupt to execution of the first instruction of the ISR when the memory being accessed has no wait states"; "Tail chaining requires 6 cycles when using zero wait state memory." [Established] ([M4 TRM](https://documentation-service.arm.com/static/5f19da2a20b7cf4bc524d99a))
- **Cortex-M0+ TRM DDI0484C:** "The worst case interrupt latency, for the highest priority active interrupt in a zero wait-state system not using jitter suppression, is 15 cycles." [Established]
- **Cortex-M23 TRM DDI0550D:** "If the Security Extension is not implemented or when a short stack is used, the interrupt latency is 15 cycles"; with a full stack (Non-secure exception interrupting Secure code) "the interrupt latency is 25 cycles." [Established]
- **Cortex-M7:** "Typically 12, worst case 14" (Arm white paper "ARM Cortex-M for Beginners", J. Yiu, March 2017, read from a copy hosted on a university course site: secondary hosting). The M52, M55 and M85 TRMs state no latency figure. [Established, secondary hosting for the M7]

- **Exception return (Cortex-M3 TRM 100165_0201_02_en r2p1 §3.9.2, same text in DDI 0337H; Cortex-M4 TRM DDI 0439B/C §3.9.1):** "Returns from interrupts similarly take twelve cycles where the instruction being returned to is fetched in parallel to the stack pop" (documentation-service.arm.com, read 21 Nov 2026 by a research subagent; the older M3 TRMs DDI 0337E/G give no return figure). [Established]

## R-308 · RTOS releases, priority inheritance and the Mars Pathfinder account

*Read on 21 Nov 2026 by a research subagent with curl (primary sources unless marked).*

- **FreeRTOS kernel:** current release V11.3.3, "Changes between FreeRTOS V11.3.2 and FreeRTOS V11.3.3 released October 29, 2026" ([History.txt at tag V11.3.3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FreeRTOS/FreeRTOS-Kernel/V11.3.3/History.txt)); earlier V11.3.2 (16 Oct 2026), V11.3.1 (Aug 2026), V11.3.0 (Mar 2026). [Established]
- **FreeRTOS LTS:** current 202604 LTS with kernel 11.3.0; "FreeRTOS long term support (LTS) releases receive security and critical bug fixes (should any be necessary) for at least two years following their release" ([LTS libraries page](https://www.freertos.org/Documentation/03-Libraries/01-Library-overview/03-LTS-libraries/01-LTS-libraries), "Last Updated: April 29, 2026"). The GitHub FreeRTOS-LTS README still describes 202406 LTS (stale). [Established]
- **FreeRTOS mutexes** ([mutex documentation](https://www.freertos.org/Documentation/02-Kernel/02-Kernel-features/02-Queues-mutexes-and-semaphores/04-Mutexes)): "if a high priority task blocks while attempting to obtain a mutex (token) that is currently held by a lower priority task, then the priority of the task holding the token is temporarily raised to that of the blocking task"; "Priority inheritance does not cure priority inversion! It just minimises its effect in some situations"; "A task remains at its highest inherited priority until it has released all the mutexes it holds." [Established]
- **Zephyr:** "Zephyr 4.5.0 2026-10-28 2027-10-28 Latest stable … Zephyr 3.7.0 (LTS3) 2024-07-26 2029-07-27 Long Term Support" ([release index](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/releases/index.html)); 4.4.0 was 2026-04-14; the next release, 4.6 (April 2027), is designated LTS4. [Established]
- **Mars Pathfinder priority inversion:** Glenn Reeves (JPL flight-software lead), 15 Dec 1997, archived in RISKS 19.54 ([RISKS 19.54](https://catless.ncl.ac.uk/Risks/19/54), secondary archive of the original email): "The higher priority bc_dist task was blocked by the much lower priority ASI/MET task that was holding a shared resource"; the fix was to "change the creation flags for the semaphore so as to enable the priority inheritance"; and, correcting an earlier account, "No, we did not use the vxWorks shell to change the software" (the patch was uploaded as a validated difference image). The earlier account is Mike Jones's RISKS 19.49 post of 7 Dec 1997 relaying a keynote by Wind River's David Wilner (landing 4 July 1997, VxWorks). [Established]

## R-312 · Hardware security: certification schemes, TrustZone-M, regulation, PUFs, attacks

*Read on 21 Nov 2026 by a research subagent with curl and pdftotext (primary unless marked). developer.arm.com, Nordic's notices and Springer pages blocked automated access; ISO/IEC 19790 is paywalled.*

- **PSA Certified** ([psacertified.org](https://www.psacertified.org/)): Level 1 is a questionnaire reviewed by a lab; Level 2 is "a laboratory evaluation of a PSA Root of Trust (PSA-RoT) to provide evidence that it can protect against scalable software attacks" (25 days); Level 3 "includes more attack types, more sophisticated side channel and perturbation attacks as well as physical attacks" (35 man-days); Level 4 iSE/SE uses "a higher attack potential (AP=25)"; Level 2 guidance: "Cryptographic keys stored in the PSA-RoT should be unique per device to prevent creation of a honeypot for physical attacks". Site counter in Nov 2026: "319 Certifications" from "124 Companies". GlobalPlatform assumed governance on 16 Sep 2025, when "more than 250" products were certified. [Established]
- **TrustZone for Armv8-M** (Arm white paper, 2015, and arm.com product pages): Secure and Non-secure states "orthogonal to the existing Thread and Handler modes"; the division "is memory map based" (SAU and IDAU) "without the need of a Secure Monitor exception handler"; entry into Secure code through an SG instruction in Non-Secure Callable memory, return with BXNS. Cores: Cortex-M23, M33, M35P (with physical-attack resilience), M55 and M85 (Armv8.1-M, adding PACBTI). Trusted Firmware-M implements the Secure Processing Environment. [Established]
- **SESIP and Common Criteria:** SESIP "has been adopted by CEN and CENELEC as a European Standard (EN 17927)" with five assurance levels based on Common Criteria (GlobalPlatform, primary); Common Criteria defines seven EALs from EAL1 "functionally tested" to EAL7 "formally verified design and tested", with vulnerability analysis rising from AVA_VAN.1 to AVA_VAN.5 (CC:2022 text); the CC portal lists 1753 certified products, 748 of them ICs and smart-card devices (Nov 2026); the EU's EUCC scheme has applied since 27 Feb 2025. [Established]
- **FIPS 140-3** (NIST CSRC): four security levels; approved 22 Mar 2019, effective 22 Sep 2019, based on ISO/IEC 19790:2012; FIPS 140-2 modules are accepted "through September 21, 2026" before moving to the Historical list (one NIST table says 22 Sep 2026; no completion notice found by 21 Nov 2026). [Established; transition wording inconsistent]
- **EU Cyber Resilience Act**, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 ([Commission page](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act) and the legal text, Article 71): in force 10 Dec 2024; reporting obligations (Article 14) from 11 Sep 2026; notified-body provisions from 11 Jun 2026; main obligations from 11 Dec 2027. Annex III Class I lists "Microcontrollers with security-related functionalities"; actively exploited vulnerabilities require an early warning within 24 hours and a notification within 72 hours; support periods "no less than five years" unless the product's lifetime is shorter. **Radio Equipment Directive** cybersecurity: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 applies from 1 Aug 2025 (per Delegated Regulation 2023/2444), with EN 18031-1/-2/-3:2024 cited in the OJ "with restrictions" on 30 Jan 2025. [Established]
- **SRAM PUFs:** introduced by Guajardo, Kumar, Schrijen and Tuyls, CHES 2007 (LNCS, pp. 63–80); Schrijen and van der Leest, DATE 2012, measured fractional Hamming distances of about 3–5% between readouts at the enrollment temperature and up to 20.5% at temperature extremes, so error correction must be sized for the worst case. Vendor slides claim a −55 to 150 °C range and ">25 years lifetime" (vendor claims). [Established; vendor claims marked]
- **Classic attack papers:** Kocher, "Timing Attacks on Implementations of Diffie-Hellman, RSA, DSS, and Other Systems", CRYPTO '96; Kocher, Jaffe and Jun, "Differential Power Analysis", CRYPTO '99, LNCS pp. 388–397; Boneh, DeMillo and Lipton, "On the Importance of Checking Cryptographic Protocols for Faults", EUROCRYPT '97, LNCS pp. 37–51. (Crossref records and author pages.) [Established]
- **MCU attack cases:** Obermaier and Tatschner, "Shedding too much Light on a Microcontroller's Firmware Protection", USENIX WOOT 2017 (STM32F0 read-out protection); Kraken Security Labs, 31 Jan 2020: voltage glitching of the STM32F205 in Trezor wallets with "just 15 minutes of physical access"; Espressif advisory and NVD CVE-2019-17391 (ESP32 eFuse read protection bypassed by a glitch after reset; CVSS 3.1 4.6, physical vector); NVD CVE-2020-27211 (nRF52840 APPROTECT bypassed by a fault during boot); Schink, Wagner, Unterstein and Heyszl, "Security and Trust in Open Source Security Tokens", TCHES 2021. [Established]
- **Roots of trust:** NIST defines them as "Highly reliable hardware, firmware, and software components that perform specific, critical security functions"; NIST SP 800-193 (May 2018) frames platform firmware resiliency as protect, detect and recover. [Established]

## R-313 · Security regulation, Cortex-M52 and Bluetooth pairing (Course 18 audit)

*Read on 21 Nov 2026 by a research subagent from EUR-Lex, Arm, ISO and Bluetooth SIG documents (unece.org and the main ISO site blocked automated access; EU and ISO committee pages were used).*

- **CRA support period (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, Art. 13(8), EUR-Lex):** "the support period shall be at least five years. Where the product with digital elements is expected to be in use for less than five years, the support period shall correspond to the expected use time." [Established]
- **CRA product classes:** Annex III Class I includes "Microprocessors with security-related functionalities" and "Microcontrollers with security-related functionalities" (items 13–14); Class II lists "Tamper-resistant microprocessors" and "Tamper-resistant microcontrollers" (items 3–4); Annex IV (critical) lists "Hardware Devices with Security Boxes", smart meter gateways, and "Smartcards or similar devices, including secure elements". [Established]
- **CRA conformity routes (Art. 32):** Class I may use internal control (module A) only where harmonised standards, common specifications or certification schemes (at least "substantial") are applied in full, otherwise module B+C or H; Class II needs B+C, H, or where available a European cybersecurity certification scheme at "substantial"; critical products need a European cybersecurity certificate where a delegated act under Art. 8(1) requires one, otherwise the Class II routes. [Established]
- **CRA reporting (Art. 14):** actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents are notified "simultaneously to the CSIRT designated as coordinator … and to ENISA … via the single reporting platform"; early warning "without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours" of becoming aware, a notification within 72 hours, and a final report no later than 14 days after a corrective measure is available (one month after the notification for incidents). [Established]
- **CRA dates (Arts. 69 and 71):** the Regulation applies from 11 December 2027, Article 14 from 11 September 2026 and Chapter IV from 11 June 2026; under Art. 69(3) the Article 14 obligations also apply to products placed on the market before 11 December 2027. [Established]
- **Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2392 of 28 November 2025 (OJ L, 1 Dec 2025):** the technical descriptions of the important and critical product categories; tamper-resistant MPUs and MCUs are designed for "protection of AVA_VAN level 2 or 3", secure elements "at least AVA_VAN.4", including TPMs and embedded UICCs. [Established]
- **Arm Cortex-M52:** announced 22 Nov 2023 (Arm Newsroom), extending "the Armv8.1-M Cortex-M line-up"; the product page lists "Optional support for Arm TrustZone technology", optional Helium and PACBTI. [Established]
- **Automotive cybersecurity:** UN Regulation No 155 (OJ L 82, 9 Mar 2021; in force 22 Jan 2021) applies to vehicle categories M and N (and O with an ECU); Regulation (EU) 2019/2144, Annex II (consolidated 7 Jul 2024), code B: refusal of new EU type-approvals from 6 July 2022 and of registration of non-compliant vehicles from 7 July 2024. ISO/SAE 21434:2021 "Road vehicles — Cybersecurity engineering", edition 1, published 2021-08 (SAE: 31 Aug 2021). [Established]
- **Bluetooth static passkeys:** Core Specification v5.4/v6.0, Vol 3 Part H §2.3.5.6.3: "The Passkey should be generated randomly during each pairing procedure and not be reused from a previous procedure. Static Passkeys should not be used since they can compromise the security of the link"; LE Secure Connections commits to the passkey's 20 bits one per round, and "A MITM attacker with only partial knowledge of the Passkey will only receive one incorrectly-guessed bit of the Passkey before the protocol fails." NIST SP 800-121 Rev. 2 (upd. 19 Jan 2022): "Static SSP passkeys facilitate MITM attacks." (That a static passkey falls to about 20 repeated pairings is an inference from the one-bit property, not a quoted figure.) [Established]

Long-term challenge: "Power scaling — no solutions left to reduce the supply voltage because of lack of steep-subthreshold devices"; near-term: GAA devices reduce the supply "but not in a sustained manner". The 2024 Executive Summary notes $V_{DD}$ was raised to 0.75 V in 2021 because of "higher than anticipated leakage of FinFET transistors". Jain et al., ISSCC 2012, paper 3.6; [Intel Labs ISSCC 2012 press overview](https://download.intel.com/newsroom/kits/isscc/2012/pdfs/ISSCC-IL-Press-Overview.pdf)): IA-32 processor in 32 nm that "Operates from 280mV @3MHz to 1.2V @915MHz", "4.7x better energy efficiency in NTV mode", "2mW minimum power". The Hot Chips 2012 slides give different bench numbers and are not used here. [Established]
- **Ambiq SPOT**: 19 Jan 2015 release, SPOT "operates transistors at sub-threshold voltages (less than 0.5V)"; [5 Mar 2026 release](https://ambiq.com/news/ambiq-reveals-12nm-spot-platform-enabling-operation-down-to-300mv-for-atomiq/), a 12 nm SPOT platform on TSMC N12e with a ULP mode "engineered to operate as low as 300mV" for the upcoming Atomiq part. [Established] for 2015; [Industry estimate] (company claim, part not yet shipping) for 2026
- **FO4 delay rule of thumb**: Ho, Mai and Horowitz, "The Future of Wires", *Proc. IEEE* 89(4), pp. 490–504, Apr. 2001: FO4 delay about 360 ps × $L_{drawn}$ (µm) at typical and 500 ps × $L_{drawn}$ under worst-case conditions; "In a 0.18-µm technology, an FO4 is about 90 pS under worst case environmental conditions"; "a FO1 is one-third a FO4". Horowitz, DAC 2000 slides: "Approximately 0.36 nS/µm*Ldrawn at TT". Harris, Ho, Wei and Horowitz, "The Fanout-of-4 Inverter Delay Metric" (Stanford manuscript) proposes FO4 "to normalize process and operating condition variations". [Established]
- **Simulated FO4 by node**: Stillmaker and Baas, *Integration, the VLSI Journal* 58, pp. 74–81, 2017, Table 2 (predictive device models, not silicon): 77.2 ps at 180 nm and 1.8 V; 34.7 ps at 130 nm and 1.2 V; 10.9 ps at 45 nm and 1.1 V; 4.02 ps at 14 nm and 0.86 V; 2.47 ps at 7 nm and 0.8 V. No foundry-published measured FO4 for a 7, 5 or 3 nm node was found. [Industry estimate]
- **Leading-node claims**: Intel, 9 Oct 2025 Panther Lake release ([intc.com](https://www.intc.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1752/intel-unveils-panther-lake-architecture-first-ai-pc)): Intel 18A delivers "up to 15% better performance per watt and 30% improved chip density compared to Intel 3" (footnote: Intel internal analysis as of February 2024). TSMC N2 (G. Yeap et al., IEDM 2024 paper 2.1, summarized in the [IEEE EDS newsletter, Apr 2025](https://www.ieee.org/ns/periodicals/EDS/EDS-APRIL-2025-HTML/InnerFiles/LandPage.html)): "a 15% speed gain (or 30% power reduction) at >1.15x chip density versus … N3", mass production scheduled for the second half of 2025. No nominal supply for N2 or 18A was found on a company page. [Industry estimate] (vendor claims)
- **SKY130 periphery rules, channel width in cells** ([periphery rules page](https://skywater-pdk.readthedocs.io/en/main/rules/periphery.html), read 24 Nov 2026): rule difftap.2b, "Minimum channel width (Diff And Poly) for FETs inside areaid.sc", 0.360 µm (against the general 0.420 µm). [Established]

## R-315 · Logic families in practice, SKY130 cells, logical effort, interconnect scaling and repeaters (Course 19)

*Read on 21 Nov 2026 by a research subagent with curl and pdftotext (tsmc.com, anandtech.com, dblp and the Semantic Scholar API blocked automated access; the TSMC A16 figures are from press reports only).*

- **Dynamic logic in processors:** Silberman et al., "A 1.0-GHz Single-Issue 64-Bit PowerPC Integer Processor", *IEEE JSSC*, Nov 1998 ([IBM Research page](https://research.ibm.com/publications/10-ghz-single-issue-64-bit-powerpc-integer-processor)): "a delayed reset dynamic circuit style enabling complex functions to be implemented in a few levels of logic". Nowka and Galambos, ICCD 1998: "highly-optimized and noise-characterized delayed-reset domino circuits were employed in the datapath elements". Sager, Hinton et al., ISSCC 2001 paper 20.6 (Pentium 4): "The fundamental logic family used in the ALUs is internally called 'Globally-Reset Self-timed Pre-charged Domino'"; the 2 GHz clock "is doubled locally to generate a 4GHz clock"; "The first six logic stages of the ALUs (3 domino and 3 static)". [Established]
- **Retreat from dynamic logic:** Stolt et al., "Design and Implementation of the POWER6 Microprocessor", *IEEE JSSC* 43(1), Jan 2008: "13 FO4 design … without the use of power-hungry dynamic circuits outside of register files and arrays"; register files "with more than 32 entries favored a dynamic circuit implementation". D. Harris, *CMOS VLSI Design* 4th ed. lecture 10 slides (2010): domino is "1.3 – 2x faster than static CMOS", "Widely used in high-performance microprocessors in 1990s when speed was king. Largely displaced by static CMOS now that power is the limiter. Still used in memories for area efficiency." No primary statement after 2015 was found. Intel patent US 7,362,621 (granted 2008): "an upsized keeper may prevent the timely discharge of current to ground when a data line has been selected." [Established]
- **SkyWater SKY130 `sky130_fd_sc_hd`** ([library repository](https://github.com/google/skywater-pdk-libs-sky130_fd_sc_hd), release 0.0.2, Nov 2020): 163 cell functions in 437 variants (count from the repository; the documentation's "approximate" table differs). `inv_1`: NMOS `nfet_01v8` W/L = 0.65/0.15 µm and PMOS `pfet_01v8_hvt` 1.0/0.15 µm (the documentation lists `pfet_01v8`). `nand2_1` and `nor2_1` use the same 0.65 and 1.0 µm devices as the inverter; higher drive strengths use parallel multiples (`m=2`, `m=4`). Drive strengths: inv _1, _2, _4, _6, _8, _12, _16; nand2 and nor2 _1, _2, _4, _8. From the netlists: `dfxtp_1` (flip-flop) and `mux4_1` (second level) use transmission gates; `mux2_1` and `dlxtp_1` do not. [Established]
- **Logical effort:** I. Sutherland, R. Sproull and D. Harris, *Logical Effort: Designing Fast CMOS Circuits*, Morgan Kaufmann, 1999 (ISBN 978-1-55860-557-2). The original paper, Sutherland and Sproull, "Logical Effort: Designing for Speed on the Back of an Envelope", appeared in *Advanced Research in VLSI*, 1991 (pages and publisher not confirmed). Harris, "Lecture 6: Logical Effort" slides (2020): NAND g = (n+2)/3, NOR g = (2n+1)/3, parasitic delay "In multiples of pinv (≈1)"; "For pinv = 1, solve numerically for ρ = 3.59"; "2.4 < ρ < 6 gives delay within 15% of optimal … I like ρ = 4"; "Delay of path is about log4F FO4 inverter delays". [Established]
- **Interconnect, IRDS 2024 More Moore** (Table MM01): node labels G48M24 (gate pitch 48 nm, M0 pitch 24 nm) in 2024 and G42M14 from 2035 (re-read from the table file, 24 Nov 2026); M0 pitch 24 nm (2024) to 14 nm (2035 on); Mx pitch 32 nm to 14 nm; tight-pitch Mx wire 300 Ω/µm (2024) and 475 Ω/µm (2025 on) with 270 aF/µm; 80 nm-pitch reference wire 13.3 Ω/µm and 198 aF/µm. Table MM-5: "Interconnect resistance has now entered an exponential increase regime because of non-ideal scaling of the barrier for Cu and increased scattering at the surface and grain-boundary interfaces." §4.5.1: Cu "expected to remain … the preferred solution … at least until 2029 while non-Cu solutions (e.g. Co and Ru) are expected to be used for the local interconnect (M0)." [Industry estimate] (roadmap)
- **Copper size effect:** D. Gall, *J. Appl. Phys.* 127, 050901 (2020): scattering "causes the resistivity of, for example, 10-nm-wide Cu interconnect lines to be approximately an order of magnitude larger than that of bulk Cu"; Cu ρ₀λ = 6.7 × 10⁻¹⁶ Ω·m², mean free path 39.9 nm (first principles). imec, 3 June 2025: "Ru lines at 16nm pitch with average resistance as low as 656 Ω /µm". [Established] (Gall); [Industry estimate] (imec)
- **Backside power:** Intel, 5 June 2023 (VLSI Symposium 2023 paper T1-1): PowerVia test chip with "standard cell utilization exceeding 90%" and "more than 5% frequency benefit in silicon due to reduced IR drop"; the press release adds "more than 30% platform voltage droop improvement". Intel 18A (9 Oct 2025 release) includes PowerVia. TSMC A16 "Super Power Rail" against N2P, from press reports (Tom's Hardware, 25 Apr 2024 and 22 Apr 2026): 8–10% speed, 15–20% lower power, 1.07–1.10× chip density, volume production now 2027. [Established] (Intel test chip); [Industry estimate] (TSMC, via press)
- **Wires and repeaters:** Ho, Mai and Horowitz, "The Future of Wires", *Proc. IEEE* 89(4), 2001: local wires "have delays that either track gate delays or grow slowly relative to gate delays"; global wire delay "will remain constant if repeaters are used, meaning that relative to gate delays, their delays scale upwards"; delay-optimal repeaters have "a driver fanout of 2.7", and a delay–power optimum makes segments "longer by 1.7×" with latency up "about 13%" and capacitance down "30%". Bakoglu and Meindl, "Optimal Interconnection Circuits for VLSI", *IEEE Trans. Electron Devices* ED-32(5), pp. 903–909, May 1985 (0–90% delays): k = √(R_int C_int/(2.3 R₀C₀)), h = √(R₀C_int/(R_int C₀)), T = 7.6√(R₀R_int C₀C_int). Harris, lecture 14 slides: about "40 ps/mm in 65 nm process" for an optimally repeated wire, and an energy premium of about 87% over an unrepeated wire. [Established]

## R-316 · Dennard scaling, leakage and DVFS, sequencing overhead and clock distribution, SRAM cells (Course 19)

*Read on 21 Nov 2026 by a research subagent with curl and pdftotext (st.com, semiwiki.com, fuse.wikichip.org and the ISSCC 2025 program were blocked or unreachable; TSMC N3/N3E/N2 SRAM figures are from trade press).*

- **Dennard scaling:** Dennard et al., "Design of ion-implanted MOSFET's with very small physical dimensions", *IEEE JSSC* 9(5), pp. 256–268, Oct 1974: under constant-field scaling "the power density remains constant. Thus, even if many more circuits are placed on a given integrated circuit chip, the cooling problem is essentially unchanged"; and already "the subthreshold behavior does not scale as desired". Horowitz et al., "Scaling, Power, and the Future of CMOS", IEDM 2005: "since kT/q does not scale and leakage currents are set by the transistor's threshold voltage, there is a limit to how low one can make a transistor's Vth … from the 130mn [sic] technology forward, Vdd has been scaling slowly, if at all"; the energy optimum "sets the leakage energy to be about 30% of the active power". Horowitz, ISSCC 2014 plenary: clock-frequency scaling "stopped in the early 2000s" because processors hit the air-cooling "power wall … around 100W" and threshold voltage could no longer scale "due to rising leakage currents". [Established]
- **DVFS operating points** (company-authored Linux device trees, mainline kernel, read Nov 2026): Rockchip RK3588 Cortex-A76 cluster 1200 MHz at 0.675 V to 2400 MHz at 1.000 V; Cortex-A55 cluster 1008 MHz at 0.675 V to 1800 MHz at 0.950 V; NXP i.MX 8M Mini Cortex-A53 1.2, 1.6 and 1.8 GHz at 0.85, 0.95 and 1.00 V. Upstream defaults, not datasheet guarantees. [Established]
- **Sequencing overhead:** Hrishikesh et al., "The Optimal Logic Depth Per Pipeline Stage is 6 to 8 FO4 Inverter Delays", ISCA 2002: latch overhead "36ps (1 FO4) at 100nm", skew 0.3 FO4 and jitter 0.5 FO4 (from Kurd et al. at 180 nm), total 1.8 FO4. Harris, *CMOS VLSI Design* slides: a buffered latch is "Rather slow (1.5 – 2 FO4 delays)"; "The typical FO4 inverter delay for a process of feature size f (in nm) is about 0.5f ps". [Established]
- **Clock distribution:** I. Young (Intel), Stanford EE380 lecture, 2005: Itanium (0.18 µm, 800 MHz) "Projected max skew without deskew mechanism = 110ps", "Max skew with deskew mechanism = 28ps"; Pentium 4 "Pre-compensation max skew ~ ±32ps", "Post-compensation max skew ±8ps", and "Deliberately skew clocks for performance – 200MHz frequency increase obtained". AMD Piledriver resonant clock mesh (ISSCC 2012): "reduce clock distribution power up to 24%"; JSSC 2013: "a peak 25% global clock power reduction at 75°C, which translates to a 4.5% reduction in average application core power". IBM POWER6 (*JSSC*, 2008): a grid fed by local H-trees; "On-chip clock tuning resulted in up to a 10% frequency improvement". [Established]
- **SKY130 flip-flop** (`sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfxtp_1`, typical corner tt_025C_1v80 Liberty, units ns and pF): clock-to-Q 0.2692 ns rise and 0.2652 ns fall at 0.01 ns clock slew and 0.0005 pF load; setup 0.0508 ns (D rising) and 0.1033 ns (D falling), hold −0.0285 and −0.0468 ns, at 0.01 ns clock and data slews; pre-layout models. [Established]
- **SRAM cells:** TSMC N5 "densest 0.021 um2 SRAM cells" (Yeap et al., IEDM 2019, title); TSMC N3E 0.021 µm² and N2 about 0.0175 µm² (38 Mb/mm²) per Tom's Hardware (31 Oct 2024, reporting TSMC's IEDM 2024 paper; its prose and table disagree on N3); Intel 18A 0.021 µm² (ISSCC 2025 paper title only). IRDS 2024: "Bitcell scaling is slowing down because of the slow-down of the device pitch and gate pitch." TSMC VLSI 2023: a 3 nm, 27.6 Mb/mm² SRAM with "0.48 - 1.2 V Wide Operating Range". SKY130 single-port bitcell `sram_sp_cell` is 1.200 × 1.580 µm; the PDK restricts its use to the provided IP. IBM POWER6 gave "voltage sensitive memory cells … a higher voltage supply (nominal at 1.25 V)" against 1.1 V logic. [Established] (N5, IRDS, SKY130, POWER6); [Industry estimate] (N3E, N2, 18A via press or titles)

## R-318 · Synthesis and STA tools, Liberty and SDC, variation models, SKY130 corners and timing margins, AI-driven implementation claims (Course 19)

*Read on 24 Nov 2026 by a research subagent and the main agent (curl and shallow git clones; api.github.com refused these repositories, so GitHub facts are pinned to commits; cadence.com and businesswire.com refused automated access and were not used directly).*

- **Yosys:** repository <https://github.com/YosysHQ/yosys>, highest tag `v0.71` ("Release version 0.71", commit dated 12 Nov 2026). README: "a framework for RTL synthesis tools"; "free software licensed under the ISC license". `abc` pass help: "This pass uses the ABC tool [1] for technology mapping of yosys's internal gate library to a target architecture"; `-liberty <file>`: "generate netlists for the specified cell library"; `-D <picoseconds>`: "set delay target". `dfflibmap` help: "Map internal flip-flop and latch cells to the flip-flop and latch cells in the technology library specified in the given liberty files." [Established]
- **ABC:** Berkeley starting page <https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~alanmi/abc/starting.htm>: "ABC combines scalable logic optimization based on And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs), optimal-delay DAG-based technology mapping for look-up tables and standard cells, and innovative algorithms for sequential synthesis and verification." [Established]
- **OpenSTA:** <https://github.com/The-OpenROAD-Project/OpenSTA> (commit `39f9dec`, 23 Nov 2026; upstream <https://github.com/parallaxsw/OpenSTA>). README: "a gate level static timing verifier"; reads "Verilog netlist", "Liberty library", "SDC timing constraints", "SDF delay annotation", "SPEF parasitics"; "dual licensed ... under GPL v3 ... and ... for commerical applications by Parallax Software". doc/Commands.md: `set_timing_derate`; on-chip variation "is the default analysis type". sdc/Variables.tcl: CRPR "The default value is 1". ChangeLog: "Release 3.2.0 2026/10/15"; 3.0.1 (2026/03/12): "Statistical timing (SSTA) with Liberty LVF (Liberty Variation Format) models is now supported"; 3.0.0 (2025/11/26) "adds multi-corner multi-mode (mcmm) support". Its example script uses "+/-10% min/max derating" (an example, not a norm). OpenSTA's documentation implements "SDC 2.1". No mention of AOCV was found. [Established]
- **SDC and Liberty governance:** Synopsys TAP-in page (<https://www.synopsys.com/community/interoperability-programs/tap-in.html>): SDC is "Used to describe the "design intent" and surrounding constraints for synthesis, clocking, timing, power, test and environmental and operating conditions", released under open-source licensing. Synopsys release, 30 Sep 2014 (<https://news.synopsys.com/2014-09-30-Synopsys-Announces-New-Additions-to-Liberty-to-Significantly-Speed-up-Timing-Closure>): "In May 2006, an industry-wide Liberty Technical Advisory Board was formed ... under the auspices of the IEEE Industry Standards and Technology Organization (IEEE-ISTO)"; AOCV, POCV and SOCV formats were consolidated into "the Liberty Variation Format (LVF) extensions", ratified "on August 1, 2014". Release of 27 Feb 2017: "three statistical moment-based extensions to the LVF standard consisting of mean shift, standard deviation and skewness". Si2 (<https://si2.org/?p=383>) lists "ECSM Timing and Power Specification v2.1.2 (contributed by Cadence Design Systems ...)". The latest Liberty Reference Manual version could not be confirmed (behind registration). [Established]
- **Variation models and corner counts:** A. B. Kahng, "New Game, New Goal Posts: A Recent History of Timing Closure," DAC 2015 (<https://vlsicad.ucsd.edu/Publications/Conferences/330/c330.pdf>): "Advanced on-chip variation (AOCV) delay derating tables have been mainstream since the 40nm foundry node"; POCV "improves on AOCV in that stage counts are no longer needed; rather, σ² terms are accumulated over a given path"; LVF provides "one number per load-slew combination per cell"; MCMM clock synthesis "in a regime where each of hundreds of scenarios has different clock insertion delay and timing constraints". A. Tetelbaum (Abelite Design Automation), "Corner-based Timing Signoff and What Is Next," 2014 (<https://anysilicon.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/Corner_based_Signoff_paper_Jan_2014a.pdf>): "design companies currently use 12-126 corners", with a prediction of 16–248 by 2020; the author's company sold signoff tools. No dated figure for 5/3 nm was found. [Industry estimate]
- **SKY130 corners and the open flow:** the `sky130_fd_sc_hd` repository's `timing/` directory holds 16 corner files: ff `100C_1v65`, `100C_1v95`, `n40C_1v56`, `n40C_1v65`, `n40C_1v76`, `n40C_1v95_ccsnoise`; ss `100C_1v40`, `100C_1v60`, `n40C_1v28`, `n40C_1v35`, `n40C_1v40`, `n40C_1v44`, `n40C_1v60_ccsnoise`, `n40C_1v76`; tt `025C_1v80`, `100C_1v80`. OpenROAD-flow-scripts (<https://github.com/The-OpenROAD-Project/OpenROAD-flow-scripts>, commit `b02bf4ae`, 23 Nov 2026) `flow/platforms/sky130hd/config.mk` loads only `sky130_fd_sc_hd__tt_025C_1v80.lib`, which declares `delay_model : "table_lookup"` (NLDM; no LVF or CCS groups found). The same assembled TT Liberty (<https://raw.githubusercontent.com/The-OpenROAD-Project/OpenROAD-flow-scripts/master/flow/platforms/sky130hd/lib/sky130_fd_sc_hd__tt_025C_1v80.lib>, read 24 Nov 2026) sets `input_threshold_pct_rise : 50`, `output_threshold_pct_rise : 50`, `slew_lower_threshold_pct_rise : 20`, `slew_upper_threshold_pct_rise : 80` (the same for fall) and `slew_derate_from_library : 1.0`. Reference-design clock periods (`flow/designs/sky130hd/*/constraint.sdc`): gcd 1.1 ns, aes 3.6 ns, jpeg 5 ns, riscv32i 6.0 ns, ibex 8.0 ns, each with I/O delays of 20% of the period; none of the five sets clock uncertainty or a timing derate. `sky130hd/microwatt` (15.0 ns) sets `set_clock_uncertainty 0.25` and derates of 0.95/1.05. Flow setup and hold repair margins default to 0. These are open-flow test settings, not foundry signoff recommendations. [Established]
- **SKY130 cell timing tables:** per-cell Liberty JSON files in <https://github.com/google/skywater-pdk-libs-sky130_fd_sc_hd/tree/main/cells> (read 24 Nov 2026 by the main agent): areas `inv_1`, `nand2_1`, `nor2_1`, `buf_1` 3.7536 µm²; `nand3_1`, `a21oi_1`, `o21ai_1` 5.0048; `nand4_1`, `and2_1` 6.256; `a22oi_1` 7.5072. NLDM tables (7 × 7, input transition 0.01–1.5 ns by load) at `tt_025C_1v80` for these cells and `inv_1` at `ss_100C_1v60` are reproduced unchanged in `courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/labs/19-10-lab/sky130_hd_subset.json` (Apache License 2.0). [Established]
- **Commercial tools:** Synopsys PrimeTime page: "As the industry's trusted golden signoff solution, PrimeTime provides comprehensive timing, signal integrity, power, and variation-aware analysis"; datasheet (06/10/26): "AOCV uses context-specific derate factors that consider location and logic depth of each path"; "POCV ... provides a lightweight statistical margining approach". Cadence Tempus launch, 20 May 2013 (EE Journal reprint <https://www.eejournal.com/industry_news/20130520-01>): a Cadence executive said "the time spent in timing closure and signoff is approaching 40 percent of the overall design implementation flow". Siemens markets Aprisa as "an RTL-to-GDS solution that offers complete synthesis and place-and-route functionality". [Vendor claim]
- **AI-driven implementation:** Synopsys release, 7 Feb 2023 (<https://news.synopsys.com/2023-02-07-AI-designed-Chips-Reach-Scale-with-First-100-Commercial-Tape-outs-Using-Synopsys-Technology>): "more than 3x productivity increases, up to 25% lower total power and significant reduction in die size"; DSO.ai "uses reinforcement learning to enhance PPA in very large solution spaces". Synopsys release, 20 Mar 2024: "a more than 10% boost in performance, power, area (PPA), up to 10X faster turn-around time ... when compared to optimization without the use of AI". Cadence Cerebrus launch, 22 Jul 2021 (design-reuse reprint <https://design-reuse.com/news/50354/cadence-ml-based-cerebrus.html>): "improve engineering productivity by up to 10X versus a manual approach while also realizing up to a 20% better power, performance and area (PPA)"; Samsung Foundry: "more than an 8% power reduction on some of our most critical blocks". Cadence release, 9 Jun 2022 (reprint <https://www.design-reuse.com/news/52118/cadence-cerebrus-intelligent-chip-explorer.html>): MediaTek "shrunk the die area by 5% and reduced power by more than 6%"; Renesas "a 75% improvement in total negative slack (TNS)". Agrawal and Bushnell lecture 14alt: "MATS+ 5n ... MARCH C- 10n". [Established]

## R-322 · The gm/ID method and its tools, open-PDK device models, published RF CMOS f_T and self-gain, IRDS 2024 OSC, analog design automation, analog respin data (Course 20)

*Read on 24 Nov 2026 by a research subagent with WebFetch and curl. IEEE Xplore, tsmc.com, cadence.com and the irds.ieee.org HTML pages refused automated access; IEEE abstracts were read through the OpenAlex and Crossref APIs (publisher abstracts), and the IRDS PDF downloaded directly. Verbatim IEEE quotes should be re-checked against Xplore when it is reachable.*

- **Origin of the method:** F. Silveira, D. Flandre, P. G. A. Jespers, "A gm/ID based methodology for the design of CMOS analog circuits and its application to the synthesis of a silicon-on-insulator micropower OTA," *IEEE JSSC* 31(9), pp. 1314–1319, Sept. 1996, DOI 10.1109/4.535416 (Crossref; author copy at people.engr.tamu.edu). Abstract: "The synthesis procedure is based on the relation between the ratio of the transconductance over dc drain current gm/ID and the normalized current ID/(W/L). The gm/ID indeed is a universal characteristic of all the transistors belonging to a same process." [Established]
- **Lookup-table book:** P. G. A. Jespers and B. Murmann, *Systematic Design of Analog CMOS Circuits: Using Pre-Computed Lookup Tables*, Cambridge University Press, 2017 (online 28 Sep, print 12 Oct 2017), DOI 10.1017/9781108125840. Free excerpt (assets.cambridge.org): the square-law error in $g_m$ "is of the order of 20–60%" in strong inversion; in moderate inversion it "may be in error by a factor of two or even more"; "moderate inversion represents a design 'sweet spot' for a variety of circuits in these technologies." Earlier monograph: P. G. A. Jespers, *The gm/ID Methodology*, Springer, 2010. [Established]
- **Open gm/ID tools** (GitHub, rendered commit pages): bmurmann/Book-on-gm-ID-design (AGPL-3.0; latest commit 6 Oct 2025; open-source starter files with lookup-table sweeps for `sky130/`, `ihp-sg13g2/` and `gf180mcuD/`, run in ngspice); dreoilin/pygmid (Apache-2.0; latest commit 26 Jan 2026; PyPI 1.2.12 of 28 Jul 2024; "a Python 3 version of the gm/ID starter kit"); medwatt/gmid "Mosplot" (Apache-2.0; latest commit 22 Sep 2026; "sizes complete circuits automatically across process corners"); ashwith/pyMOSChar (dormant since 30 Jun 2017); iic-jku/analog-circuit-design (Apache-2.0, gm/ID notebooks on IHP SG13G2, active 24 Nov 2026). Murmann's SKY130 README (edited 1 Jun 2025): "the pfet models look non-physical in moderate and weak inversion. These models should probably not be used for designs with VGS−Vt < 150 mV." [Established]
- **Open-PDK device models:** SKY130 `nfet_01v8`/`pfet_01v8` model cards (google/skywater-pdk-libs-sky130_fd_pr): "level = 54.0 / version = 4.5" (BSIM4), `lmin = 1.5e-07`, `toxe = 4.148e-09` (n) and `4.23e-09` (p), `epsrox = 3.9`; installed for ngspice by open_pdks. GF180MCU `nmos_3p3` (models/ngspice/sm141064.ngspice): BSIM4 4.5, `lmin = 2.8e-007`, `toxe = 8e-009`. [Established]
- **Published peak NMOS f_T / f_MAX** (abstracts via OpenAlex): C.-H. Jan et al., IEDM 2010: "The peak cut-off frequency (fT) doubles from 209 GHz in the 90 nm node to 445 GHz at the 32 nm node." M.-T. Yang et al., VLSI Technology 2011 (28 nm LP bulk): "peak fT/Fmax of 349/265GHz for NMOS". S. Ong et al., RFIC 2018 (22FDX): "The best performance for nFET/pFET fT is 347/275 GHz and for fMAX is 371/299 GHz." B. Sell et al., IEDM 2017 (Intel 22FFL): NMOS 230/284 GHz; H.-J. Lee et al., IEDM 2018: "ft and fmax of NMOS above 300 GHz and 450 GHz". S. Jagar et al., *IEEE TED* 65(1), 2018 (GF 14 nm FinFET): 314/180 GHz (single-side gate contact). A. Razavieh et al., *IEEE JEDS* 9, 2021 (12 nm): "FT/FMAX of 305GHz/ 315GHz". S. S. Parihar et al., *IEEE JEDS* 11, 2023 (5 nm): "a single gate contacted n-FinFET RF device exhibits a cutoff and maximum oscillation frequency of ~100 GHz and ~170 GHz". Foundry RF figures for 6/5/4/3 nm were NOT CONFIRMED. [Established] per data point; the "plateau" reading is the chapter's [Industry estimate].
